L15.T1.A1.skill_title: Define reaction rate, apply collision theory, and explain factors affecting rate
L15.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 4 lifted-style, 16 fresh. Reaction rate definition, collision theory (frequency, energy, orientation), factors: concentration, surface area, temperature, catalyst, pressure (gases).

items.question: Define REACTION RATE.
items.expectedAnswer: Reaction rate is the change in concentration of a reactant (decrease) or product (increase) per unit time, e.g. rate = −Δ[reactant]/Δt = +Δ[product]/Δt. SI unit: mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.
items.explanation: Rate = Δ[species]/Δt. Reactants: negative sign (consumed). Products: positive (formed). Always reported as positive.

items.question: State COLLISION THEORY of reaction rates.
items.expectedAnswer: For a reaction to occur, particles must COLLIDE with: (1) sufficient kinetic energy (≥ activation energy, Ea), AND (2) the correct ORIENTATION. Only such 'effective' collisions lead to products. The rate of reaction depends on the FREQUENCY of effective collisions.
items.explanation: Three requirements: collision (frequency) + sufficient energy (≥ Ea) + correct orientation. Effective collisions ⇒ reaction.

items.question: How does INCREASING THE CONCENTRATION of reactants affect the reaction rate? Explain using collision theory.
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing concentration INCREASES the rate. More particles per unit volume ⇒ more frequent collisions per unit time ⇒ more effective collisions per second ⇒ faster rate.
items.explanation: More particles → more collisions → more effective collisions per second → higher rate.

items.question: How does INCREASING the SURFACE AREA of a solid reactant affect the reaction rate?
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing surface area INCREASES the rate. More surface ⇒ more reactant particles exposed to the other reactant ⇒ more frequent collisions ⇒ faster rate. E.g. powdered solid reacts faster than the same mass as a single lump.
items.explanation: Powder > granules > lump. More surface area means more collision sites.

items.question: How does INCREASING the TEMPERATURE affect the reaction rate? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing T greatly INCREASES the rate. At higher T: (1) particles have more KE ⇒ collide more frequently AND (2) a LARGER FRACTION of particles have KE ≥ Ea ⇒ more effective collisions. The Ea-related effect dominates: typically rate doubles for every ~10°C increase.
items.explanation: T ↑ → both frequency ↑ AND fraction with KE ≥ Ea ↑. Rate goes up sharply.

items.question: What is the role of a CATALYST in a reaction? How does it affect the rate?
items.expectedAnswer: A catalyst provides an ALTERNATIVE REACTION PATHWAY with a LOWER activation energy (Ea). More particles can exceed the lower Ea ⇒ more effective collisions per second ⇒ faster rate. The catalyst is not consumed (regenerated at the end). It does NOT change ΔH or the equilibrium position, only the rate.
items.explanation: Catalyst: alternative pathway, lower Ea, faster rate. Doesn't change equilibrium or ΔH.

items.question: How does INCREASING the PRESSURE of a GASEOUS reaction affect the rate?
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing pressure (at constant T) compresses the gas, INCREASING the concentration (more particles per unit volume) ⇒ more frequent collisions ⇒ faster rate. For solids and liquids, pressure has negligible effect.
items.explanation: Pressure ↑ ⇒ effective [gas] ↑ ⇒ more collisions ⇒ faster.

items.question: What is ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea)?
items.expectedAnswer: Activation energy is the MINIMUM kinetic energy that colliding particles must have for a successful (effective) reaction to occur. It's the energy barrier between reactants and products. Below Ea, collisions bounce off without reacting.
items.explanation: Ea: minimum energy for reaction. Sets the 'threshold' for effective collisions.

items.question: A learner says: 'A catalyst increases the kinetic energy of the reactant particles.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. A catalyst does NOT change the kinetic energy of the particles (KE depends on temperature). A catalyst provides a LOWER-Ea pathway, so more particles can exceed Ea with their existing KE. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is unchanged.
items.explanation: Catalyst lowers Ea, doesn't raise KE. Common misconception.

items.question: Why does breaking a solid into smaller pieces speed up its reaction with a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Breaking the solid into smaller pieces INCREASES its SURFACE AREA exposed to the liquid. More surface area ⇒ more contact between reactant particles ⇒ more frequent effective collisions per second ⇒ faster rate.
items.explanation: Powder = much more surface area than lump. More reactive surface = faster reaction.

items.question: A reaction takes 200 s at 25°C. At 35°C the same reaction (same amounts) takes about 100 s. Explain why.
items.expectedAnswer: At higher temperature, particles have MORE KE, so MORE particles exceed the activation energy. The fraction of effective collisions increases ⇒ the reaction proceeds faster ⇒ shorter time. The rule of thumb is that rate roughly doubles per 10°C increase, which fits this data.
items.explanation: T ↑ ⇒ exponentially more particles cross Ea ⇒ rate ↑. ~10°C ≈ ×2 rule.

items.question: What does the term EFFECTIVE COLLISION mean?
items.expectedAnswer: An effective collision is one that LEADS to a chemical reaction (i.e. forms products). The colliding particles must have KE ≥ Ea AND the correct orientation. Most collisions are NOT effective — they just bounce off.
items.explanation: Effective collision = enough energy AND correct orientation. Most collisions are ineffective.

items.question: A reaction: 2HCl(aq) + Mg(s) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Predict the EFFECT on the rate of (a) doubling [HCl]; (b) using Mg powder instead of a strip; (c) heating the system.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Doubles (or roughly doubles) the rate — more frequent collisions between HCl and Mg. (b) Increases the rate substantially — much greater surface area on Mg. (c) Increases the rate — higher KE, more particles above Ea.
items.explanation: Three factors: concentration, surface area, temperature. All increase rate when increased.

items.question: A learner says: 'Doubling the concentration of a reactant always doubles the rate.' Is this strictly correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Not strictly — it depends on the reaction order. If the reaction is FIRST ORDER in that reactant, doubling concentration doubles the rate. If SECOND order, doubling quadruples it. If ZERO order, no change. The qualitative direction (more concentration → faster) is right, but the exact factor depends on order. In CAPS, first-order behaviour is the usual assumption.
items.explanation: Rate ∝ [reactant]ⁿ. n = 1: doubles. n = 2: quadruples. n = 0: unchanged.

items.question: Two reactions with the same Ea proceed at different temperatures: 25°C and 45°C. At which temperature do MORE particles have KE ≥ Ea? Why?
items.expectedAnswer: At 45°C. Higher temperature ⇒ the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of KE shifts to higher energies AND broadens, so a larger fraction of particles have KE ≥ Ea. This is the main reason rate increases sharply with temperature.
items.explanation: T ↑: distribution shifts right, more particles past Ea ⇒ more effective collisions.

items.question: Sketch (or describe) the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures (T₁ < T₂) and indicate the activation energy Ea.
items.expectedAnswer: Description: Both curves are bell-shaped, peaking and tailing off at high KE. At higher T₂: the curve is BROADER (shifted to the right and flatter). Mark Ea on the x-axis. The AREA UNDER the curve to the right of Ea represents the fraction of particles with KE ≥ Ea — larger area at T₂ than T₁.
items.explanation: Maxwell-Boltzmann: shifts right and broadens at higher T. Fraction past Ea increases.

items.question: Explain WHY a CATALYST does NOT change the EQUILIBRIUM position.
items.expectedAnswer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of BOTH the forward AND the reverse reactions by the SAME amount. So it increases both rates equally, leaving the equilibrium constant Kc and the equilibrium concentrations unchanged. It only accelerates the approach TO equilibrium.
items.explanation: Catalyst lowers Ea equally on both sides. Same Kc, same equilibrium position, just faster to get there.

items.question: Which of the following will NOT affect the reaction rate?
options: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
Adding more of an inert gas at constant volume (gas-phase reaction)
items.expectedAnswer: Adding more of an inert gas at constant volume (gas-phase reaction)
items.explanation: Inert gas at constant V doesn't change partial pressure/concentration of reactants. No effect on rate.

items.question: Why does combustion of paper burn faster when the paper is shredded vs. as a single sheet?
items.expectedAnswer: Shredded paper has much greater surface area exposed to oxygen. More surface area ⇒ more contact between paper (fuel) and O₂ (reactant) ⇒ more collisions per second ⇒ faster combustion. (Same reason flour dust can explode but a flour bag won't.)
items.explanation: Surface area effect again. Powders/finely divided solids react MUCH faster than bulk.

items.question: List THREE factors that can be changed to INCREASE the rate of a reaction.
items.expectedAnswer: Any three of: (1) Increase concentration of reactants (or pressure for gases); (2) Increase temperature; (3) Increase surface area of solids (e.g. powder vs lump); (4) Add a catalyst; (5) Increase intensity of light (for photochemical reactions).
items.explanation: Five typical factors. CAPS expects four main ones (concentration, T, surface area, catalyst).

L15.T1.A2.skill_title: Calculate reaction rates from data and graphs
L15.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 3 lifted-style, 17 fresh. Average and instantaneous rates from concentration-time, mass-time, volume-time graphs; stoichiometric rate ratios.

items.question: Define AVERAGE RATE and INSTANTANEOUS RATE of a reaction.
items.expectedAnswer: Average rate: change in concentration of a species over a TIME INTERVAL: Δ[species]/Δt. Calculated from the slope of a SECANT line between two points on a concentration-time graph. Instantaneous rate: rate at a SPECIFIC INSTANT, calculated from the slope of the TANGENT line at that point on the curve.
items.explanation: Average = secant (over an interval). Instantaneous = tangent (at a point).

items.question: In a reaction A → B, [A] decreases from 0.50 mol·dm⁻³ to 0.30 mol·dm⁻³ over 40 s. Calculate the average rate of consumption of A.
items.explanation: Rate = −Δ[A]/Δt = −(0.30 − 0.50)/40 = 0.20/40 = 0.005 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. (Reported as positive.)

items.question: For the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: if the rate of NH₃ formation is 0.020 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹, what is the rate of N₂ consumption?
items.explanation: Rate ratios from stoichiometry: (1/coeff) × (rate of that species). Rate(N₂) = (1/2) × Rate(NH₃) = (1/2)(0.020) = 0.010 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. (For every 2 NH₃ formed, 1 N₂ is consumed.)

items.question: Continuing: for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ with rate(NH₃ formation) = 0.020 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹, what is the rate of H₂ consumption?
items.explanation: Rate(H₂) = (3/2) × Rate(NH₃) = (3/2)(0.020) = 0.030 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. (For every 2 NH₃ formed, 3 H₂ consumed.)

items.question: In a reaction producing a gas, the volume of gas collected over time is tracked. How would you calculate the average rate of gas production?
items.expectedAnswer: Average rate = ΔV/Δt (volume change per time interval) — typically in cm³·s⁻¹ or dm³·min⁻¹. Alternatively, convert to moles using PV = nRT (or at STP, 1 mol of gas = 24 dm³ at 25°C) and report in mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.
items.explanation: Volume-vs-time data: rate = ΔV/Δt. Convert to moles if needed.

items.question: A reaction produces 80 cm³ of H₂ gas in 40 s. Calculate the average rate of H₂ production (in cm³·s⁻¹).
items.explanation: Rate = 80 cm³ / 40 s = 2 cm³·s⁻¹.

items.question: On a concentration-time graph, why does the slope (rate) get LESS STEEP as the reaction progresses?
items.expectedAnswer: As the reaction proceeds, the reactant concentration decreases. Lower [reactant] ⇒ fewer collisions per unit time ⇒ lower rate. The slope of [reactant]-vs-time flattens out as [reactant] approaches zero (or its equilibrium value). For [product] vs time, the slope also decreases as the reaction slows down.
items.explanation: Rate ∝ [reactant] (for first-order at least). [reactant] ↓ as reaction proceeds ⇒ rate ↓.

items.question: On a concentration-time graph, what does a HORIZONTAL portion represent?
items.expectedAnswer: A horizontal portion (zero slope) means the concentration is not changing — either the reaction has reached EQUILIBRIUM (for a reversible reaction) or has COMPLETED (irreversible, all reactant consumed). The rate of net change is zero.
items.explanation: Flat line = rate = 0. Either equilibrium reached or reaction complete.

items.question: A mass-time graph for the decomposition of 5.0 g of a reactant shows the mass at t = 0 is 5.0 g and at t = 50 s is 3.5 g. Calculate the average rate of mass loss.
Why is the rate of a reaction usually GREATEST at the START?
items.expectedAnswer: At the start, reactant concentrations are at their HIGHEST. High concentration ⇒ many particles per unit volume ⇒ many collisions per second ⇒ many effective collisions per second ⇒ fast rate. As reaction proceeds, concentration decreases and so does the rate.
items.explanation: Initial rate is fastest because reactant concentrations are highest.

items.question: For 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), the rate of O₂ formation is 0.012 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. Calculate the rate of H₂O₂ consumption.
items.explanation: Stoichiometry 2:1. Rate(H₂O₂) = 2 × Rate(O₂) = 2 × 0.012 = 0.024 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.

items.question: A learner reports the rate of a reactant's CONSUMPTION as −0.05 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. What's wrong with this answer?
items.expectedAnswer: The rate is conventionally reported as a POSITIVE value, regardless of whether it's the rate of consumption (reactant) or formation (product). The negative sign comes from −Δ[reactant]/Δt = positive. The learner should report 0.05 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹ (positive).
items.explanation: Rate convention: always positive. The negative-sign is absorbed when defining rate of consumption.

items.question: A reaction A + B → C produces 0.040 mol of C in 0.5 dm³ over 20 s. Calculate the rate of C formation in mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.
items.explanation: [C] formed = 0.040/0.5 = 0.080 mol·dm⁻³ over 20 s. Rate = 0.080/20 = 0.004 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.

items.question: For 2A + B → 3C in a 1 dm³ container: if 0.30 mol of C forms in 60 s, what are the rates of (a) A consumption, (b) B consumption, (c) C formation?
items.expectedAnswer: [C] formed = 0.30 mol·dm⁻³. Rate of C formation = 0.30/60 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. (a) Rate(A) = (2/3) × Rate(C) = (2/3)(5.0×10⁻³) ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻³ mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. (b) Rate(B) = (1/3) × Rate(C) ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻³ mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.
items.explanation: Apply stoichiometric ratios. Rate ratios = coefficient ratios.

items.question: On a graph of [product] vs time, the curve starts at zero, rises sharply, and levels off horizontally. What does each phase tell you about the rate?
items.expectedAnswer: Rising sharply (steep slope) at t = 0: HIGH rate (high reactant concentration). Curve flattening: rate is DECREASING (reactant being consumed). Horizontal final part: rate ≈ 0 (reaction complete or at equilibrium).
items.explanation: Slope = rate. Steeper = faster. Flat = stopped/equilibrium.

items.question: In a reaction H₂ + I₂ → 2HI, [H₂] drops from 1.0 to 0.6 mol·dm⁻³ in 30 s. Find the rate of HI formation.
items.explanation: Rate(H₂ consumption) = 0.4/30 ≈ 0.01333 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹. Stoichiometry 1:2 (HI to H₂). Rate(HI formation) = 2 × Rate(H₂) = 2 × 0.01333 ≈ 0.0267 mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.

items.question: Why are rates often reported using INITIAL RATES in experiments?
items.expectedAnswer: At t = 0, only the forward reaction occurs (no products yet, so reverse rate = 0). The initial rate is straightforward to measure and depends only on the initial concentrations and conditions. Initial rates allow comparison between experiments and reveal the rate law (e.g. how rate depends on [reactant]).
items.explanation: Initial rate: only forward direction active. Clean dependence on initial conditions.

items.question: A reaction CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ produces 240 cm³ of CO₂ in 60 s at room conditions (24 dm³/mol). Calculate the average rate of CaCO₃ consumption in mol·s⁻¹.
items.explanation: n(CO₂) = 240/24 000 = 0.010 mol. From 1:1 stoich CaCO₃:CO₂: n(CaCO₃ consumed) = 0.010 mol. Rate = 0.010/60 ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻⁴ mol·s⁻¹.

items.question: Sketch (or describe) the shape of a concentration-vs-time graph for a REACTANT in an irreversible reaction.
items.expectedAnswer: Starts at the initial reactant concentration on the y-axis. Decreases over time; initially STEEP (fast rate due to high [reactant]) and gradually LESS STEEP (slowing as concentration drops). Approaches zero asymptotically (or goes to zero at completion). Curve is concave-up (decreasing curvature).
items.explanation: Typical exponential-decay-like shape for reactants. Initially steep, gradually flattens.

items.question: For the reaction 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ (rusting), if the rate of O₂ consumption is 6 × 10⁻⁴ mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹, find the rate of Fe₂O₃ formation.
items.explanation: Stoichiometry: 3 O₂ : 2 Fe₂O₃. Rate(Fe₂O₃) = (2/3) × Rate(O₂) = (2/3)(6×10⁻⁴) = 4 × 10⁻⁴ mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_STOICH_RATE: Wrong stoichiometric ratio for rates of different species
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RATE_SLOPE_CHANGE: Doesn't link slope changes to changing rate
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_HORIZONTAL_GRAPH: Misreads horizontal portion of conc-time graph

L16.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 3 lifted-style, 17 fresh. Identify London (dispersion), dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding interactions in given compounds from structure.

items.question: Name the THREE types of intermolecular forces (IMFs) covered in CAPS Physical Sciences.
items.expectedAnswer: (1) LONDON forces (also called dispersion forces or instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces); (2) DIPOLE-DIPOLE forces (between permanent dipoles in polar molecules); (3) HYDROGEN BONDING (a special, strong dipole-dipole between an H attached to N, O or F and another N/O/F).
items.explanation: London (in all molecules), dipole-dipole (polar molecules), hydrogen bonding (H attached to N/O/F).

items.question: Identify the strongest intermolecular force present in liquid H₂O.
items.expectedAnswer: Hydrogen bonding
items.explanation: H is bonded to O (an N/O/F atom) ⇒ hydrogen bonding possible. H-bonding is the strongest of the three IMFs present in water.

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid CH₄ (methane)?
items.expectedAnswer: Only LONDON (dispersion) forces. CH₄ is a non-polar molecule (symmetric tetrahedral C-H bonds, no net dipole) — so no dipole-dipole forces. H is bonded to C (not N/O/F) — so no hydrogen bonding. Just London forces between methane molecules.
items.explanation: Non-polar tetrahedral methane: London only.

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid HCl?
items.expectedAnswer: London forces AND dipole-dipole forces. HCl is a POLAR molecule (Cl is more electronegative than H, so the molecule has a permanent dipole). However, H is bonded to Cl (not N/O/F), so NO hydrogen bonding.
items.explanation: Polar molecules have London + dipole-dipole. H-bonding requires H on N/O/F — Cl doesn't qualify in CAPS.

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid NH₃ (ammonia)?
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole + HYDROGEN BONDING. NH₃ is polar (N pulls electron density), and H is bonded to N — so hydrogen bonding occurs (N-H...N type).
items.explanation: Polar + H bonded to N ⇒ all three IMFs. H-bonding is the strongest.

items.question: A student says: 'All POLAR molecules have hydrogen bonding.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. Polar molecules have dipole-dipole forces. Hydrogen bonding additionally requires an H atom bonded DIRECTLY to N, O, or F. For example, HCl is polar but does not have H-bonding (H is on Cl, not N/O/F). H₂S is polar but does not H-bond (H is on S).
items.explanation: Polar ⇒ dipole-dipole. H-bonding requires the H-on-N/O/F structural feature in addition.

items.question: A student says: 'Non-polar molecules don't have any intermolecular forces.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. ALL molecules (polar or non-polar) have LONDON (dispersion) forces. These arise from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution. Polar molecules ADDITIONALLY have dipole-dipole; H-bonders have H-bonding too. But London is universal.
items.explanation: London is in EVERY molecule. Non-polar molecules have only London (no dipole-dipole or H-bonding).

items.question: Identify the IMFs present in each: (a) Cl₂; (b) H₂O; (c) CH₃OH; (d) CO₂.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Cl₂: London only (non-polar, symmetric); (b) H₂O: London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (H on O); (c) CH₃OH (methanol): London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (H on O of -OH); (d) CO₂: London only (linear, non-polar — although C=O bonds are polar, the symmetric linear shape cancels the net dipole).
items.explanation: Check polarity (shape matters!) + check H on N/O/F. CO₂ is a classic non-polar despite polar bonds.

items.question: Which of the following CAN form hydrogen bonds with itself: CH₃OH, CH₃Br, CH₃F, CH₃NH₂, CH₃COOH?
items.expectedAnswer: CH₃OH (alcohol; H on O), CH₃NH₂ (amine; H on N), and CH₃COOH (carboxylic acid; H on O of -COOH) can form H-bonds. CH₃Br: H bonded to C, not N/O/F. CH₃F: H bonded to C (the F is not bonded to H); doesn't H-bond with itself, although CH₃F can ACCEPT H-bonds from H-bond donors via F.
items.explanation: H-bond donor needs H bonded to N/O/F. Check each structure for such an H.

items.question: Which intermolecular force is the WEAKEST in general?
items.expectedAnswer: London (dispersion)
items.explanation: Strength ranking: H-bonding > dipole-dipole > London (within similar molecular sizes). London is the weakest per pair of molecules, BUT for large non-polar molecules, total London can be larger than dipole-dipole on smaller polar molecules.

items.question: Why do LONDON forces increase in strength as the molecule grows larger?
items.expectedAnswer: London forces arise from temporary, instantaneous dipoles created by electron movement. Larger molecules have MORE electrons (more polarisable) AND more SURFACE AREA for contact between molecules ⇒ stronger and more numerous temporary dipoles ⇒ stronger London forces overall.
items.explanation: More electrons + more surface contact ⇒ stronger London. Long alkanes can have very strong total London despite being non-polar.

items.question: Determine the IMFs in liquid CH₃CHO (ethanal/acetaldehyde).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole. The C=O bond is polar (O more electronegative than C), and the asymmetric shape gives a net dipole, so the molecule is polar. However, the H atoms are bonded to C, NOT to N/O/F, so NO hydrogen bonding (in the classical sense).
items.explanation: Aldehyde: polar (C=O dipole), but no H-on-O so no H-bonding.

items.question: Why does HF form unusually strong hydrogen bonds?
items.expectedAnswer: F is the most electronegative atom; the H-F bond is very polar (H carries a large δ+ and F a large δ−). This creates very strong attraction between F (with its lone pairs) on one molecule and the H on another. So H-bonding in HF is exceptionally strong, leading to HF's anomalously high boiling point (~20°C) for a small molecule.
items.explanation: Strongest electronegativity difference + small atomic size of F ⇒ very strong H-bonds.

items.question: Identify the IMFs present between two molecules of CH₃OCH₃ (dimethyl ether).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole. The C-O-C structure has a net dipole (O carries δ−, the alkyl C's have δ+), so the molecule is polar ⇒ dipole-dipole. The H atoms are bonded to C, not to O directly — so NO hydrogen bonding within ether molecules. (Note: ethers can act as H-bond ACCEPTORS for water etc., but pure ether doesn't self-H-bond.)
items.explanation: Ether: polar molecule, but no H-on-O ⇒ no self-H-bonding. London + dipole-dipole.

items.question: A learner draws a hydrogen bond between two CH₃Cl molecules. Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. CH₃Cl is a polar molecule, but the H atoms are bonded to C (not to N/O/F). Hydrogen bonding requires an H directly bonded to N, O, or F. So CH₃Cl does NOT form hydrogen bonds; only London + dipole-dipole interactions are present.
items.explanation: H-on-Cl or H-on-C doesn't qualify for H-bonding in CAPS.

items.question: List the IMFs in propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole + HYDROGEN BONDING. The -OH group provides H bonded to O ⇒ H-bonding. The molecule is also polar ⇒ dipole-dipole. London forces present in all molecules.
items.explanation: Alcohol: -OH ⇒ H-bonding capable. All three IMFs present.

items.question: Why does CO₂ (linear) have NO net dipole moment despite having polar C=O bonds?
items.expectedAnswer: CO₂ has TWO C=O bond dipoles pointing in OPPOSITE directions (O=C=O linear structure). The two dipoles CANCEL each other vectorially, giving zero net dipole moment. So CO₂ is a NON-POLAR molecule despite having polar bonds.
items.explanation: Symmetry can cancel bond dipoles. Linear CO₂: O=C=O bonds opposite ⇒ cancel.

items.question: Which has STRONGER intermolecular forces: CH₃CH₂CH₃ (propane) or CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol)?
items.expectedAnswer: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) has stronger IMFs. Both molecules are similar in size (London forces are comparable). Propane has only London. Ethanol additionally has dipole-dipole AND hydrogen bonding (from -OH). H-bonding is much stronger than London, so ethanol has overall stronger IMFs ⇒ much higher boiling point (~78°C vs −42°C).
items.explanation: H-bonding dominates between molecules of similar size. Ethanol > propane in IMF strength.

items.question: True or False: 'A small polar molecule (like HCl) has stronger IMFs than a long non-polar molecule (like decane, C₁₀H₂₂).' Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: FALSE. While HCl has dipole-dipole forces in addition to London, decane is a much LARGER molecule with many more electrons and much more surface area for London contact. Long-chain non-polar molecules can have very strong CUMULATIVE London forces — often stronger than the IMFs of small polar molecules. This is why decane (BP ≈ 174°C) has a much higher BP than HCl (BP ≈ −85°C).
items.explanation: Size of London matters: cumulative London on a long chain can outweigh dipole-dipole on a small polar molecule.

items.question: Why does HF have a higher boiling point than HCl, despite Cl being heavier than F?
items.expectedAnswer: HF can form HYDROGEN BONDS (H bonded to F, a small electronegative atom). HCl has only London + dipole-dipole (Cl doesn't qualify for H-bonding under CAPS). H-bonding in HF is much stronger than the IMFs in HCl, so more energy is needed to vaporise HF ⇒ higher BP. (HF BP ≈ 20°C; HCl BP ≈ −85°C.)
items.explanation: H-bonding in HF >> London + dipole-dipole in HCl. H-bonding wins despite HF being smaller.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_HBONDING_REQUIREMENTS: Doesn't apply 'H bonded to N/O/F' rule for H-bonding
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_NONPOLAR_IMF: Believes non-polar molecules have no IMFs
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_POLAR_IMF: Doesn't recognise dipole-dipole in polar molecules
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_LONDON_UNIVERSAL: Doesn't recognise London is present in all molecules
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SHAPE_POLARITY: Misuses molecular shape to determine polarity
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_LONDON_SIZE_DEPENDENCE: Doesn't recognise London grows with molecular size
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BOND_VS_MOLECULAR_DIPOLE: Confuses bond dipole with molecular dipole
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_IMF_RANKING: Wrong overall IMF ranking between molecules

L16.T1.A2.skill_title: Relate intermolecular forces to physical properties
L16.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 2 lifted-style, 18 fresh. Predict and explain trends in BP, MP, vapour pressure, surface tension, and solubility based on IMF strength.

items.question: How does INCREASING the strength of IMFs affect the BOILING POINT of a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Stronger IMFs ⇒ HIGHER boiling point. More energy (heat) is needed to overcome the intermolecular attractions and vaporise the liquid into a gas.
items.explanation: Stronger IMF = more energy to separate molecules = higher BP.

items.question: How does INCREASING the strength of IMFs affect the VAPOUR PRESSURE of a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Stronger IMFs ⇒ LOWER vapour pressure (at a given T). Molecules are held more tightly together ⇒ fewer escape into the gas phase ⇒ lower equilibrium vapour pressure.
items.explanation: Vapour pressure measures escaping tendency. Stronger IMF = less escape = lower VP.

items.question: Compare the boiling points of CH₄, NH₃, and H₂O. Which has the highest BP and why?
items.expectedAnswer: H₂O has the highest BP, followed by NH₃, then CH₄. CH₄ (non-polar): only London. NH₃ (polar, has H-bonding): London + dipole-dipole + H-bonding. H₂O (polar, has H-bonding to 2 lone pairs on O): even more extensive H-bonding (each H₂O can form up to 4 H-bonds). The H-bonding network in H₂O is stronger and more extensive than in NH₃.
items.explanation: H₂O > NH₃ > CH₄. BP: 100°C > −33°C > −162°C. H₂O's tetrahedral H-bonding network is exceptional.

items.question: Why is the BOILING POINT of butane HIGHER than that of methane?
items.expectedAnswer: Butane and methane are both alkanes with only London forces (non-polar). Butane is a LARGER molecule with more electrons and more surface area for contact ⇒ STRONGER cumulative London forces ⇒ higher boiling point. (CH₄: −162°C; butane: ~−1°C.)
items.explanation: Larger molecule ⇒ stronger London. Within alkane series, BP rises with chain length.

items.question: How does INCREASING the strength of IMFs affect the SURFACE TENSION of a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Stronger IMFs ⇒ HIGHER surface tension. Molecules at the surface are pulled inward (no neighbours above) by IMFs from neighbouring molecules; this contraction creates a surface 'skin'. Stronger IMFs = stronger inward pull = higher surface tension. Water has unusually high surface tension because of H-bonding.
items.explanation: Surface tension ∝ IMF strength. Water 'beads up' more than oil because H-bonding > London.

items.question: How does a SOLUTE'S IMF compatibility with the SOLVENT affect SOLUBILITY?
items.expectedAnswer: 'Like dissolves like.' A solute dissolves best in a solvent with SIMILAR types of IMFs. Polar solutes (e.g. salt, sugar) dissolve well in polar solvents (e.g. water — H-bonding). Non-polar solutes (e.g. fats, oils) dissolve in non-polar solvents (e.g. hexane — London only). Mismatched IMFs cause poor solubility (e.g. oil and water don't mix).
items.explanation: Solubility rule: like dissolves like. Same IMF type means good mixing.

items.question: Why is the boiling point of ETHANOL much higher than that of DIETHYL ETHER, even though they have similar molecular masses?
items.expectedAnswer: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) has hydrogen bonding (H bonded to O of -OH). Diethyl ether (CH₃CH₂-O-CH₂CH₃) has no -OH so NO hydrogen bonding — only London + dipole-dipole. H-bonding is much stronger, so ethanol has a much higher BP (~78°C vs ether ~35°C) despite comparable molecular size.
items.explanation: H-bonding vs no H-bonding at similar size: H-bonding wins. Standard alcohol vs ether comparison.

items.question: Why does ICE have a LOWER DENSITY than liquid water?
items.expectedAnswer: In ice, water molecules arrange in an OPEN, HEXAGONAL LATTICE held by hydrogen bonds. This rigid 3D network spaces molecules further apart than in liquid water, where molecules can move around and pack more closely (despite still having H-bonding). So ice has LOWER density than liquid water — that's why ice floats. This anomaly is due to the directional nature of H-bonding in water.
items.explanation: Hydrogen-bonded crystal structure of ice has open hexagonal arrangement ⇒ less dense than liquid water.

items.question: Rank the following in order of INCREASING boiling point: methane, ammonia, water.
items.expectedAnswer: Methane < ammonia < water. CH₄ (London only): BP = −162°C. NH₃ (H-bonding to N): BP = −33°C. H₂O (H-bonding to O, more extensive): BP = 100°C. Water's extensive H-bonding network gives it the highest BP despite being a small molecule.
items.explanation: IMF strength: London (CH₄) < H-bonding (NH₃) < extensive H-bonding (H₂O).

items.question: A learner says: 'Stronger IMFs always lead to higher vapour pressure.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — the reverse is true. Stronger IMFs hold molecules tightly in the liquid, making it HARDER for them to escape into the gas phase. So stronger IMFs lead to LOWER vapour pressure (at a given temperature).
items.explanation: Common misconception. Vapour pressure ∝ ease of escape (inverse of IMF strength).

items.question: Why is sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) HIGHLY soluble in water but NOT in hexane (C₆H₁₄)?
items.expectedAnswer: Sugar has many -OH groups (hydroxyl), so it forms extensive HYDROGEN BONDS with water (also full of -OH). 'Like dissolves like' applies. Hexane is a non-polar alkane with only London forces — incompatible with the polar/H-bonding character of sugar, so sugar barely dissolves in hexane.
items.explanation: Sugar has many H-bonding sites ⇒ readily H-bonds with water. Hexane: no H-bonding, no polarity, can't accommodate sugar.

items.question: Why is oil insoluble in water?
items.expectedAnswer: Oil is non-polar (London forces only). Water is polar with H-bonding. Mixing them would require breaking up water's H-bonding network without providing equivalent attractions to oil. Energetically unfavourable. So oil and water do not mix — they separate into two phases.
items.explanation: 'Like dissolves like.' Non-polar + polar = incompatible.

items.question: Compare boiling points of CH₃F (methyl fluoride) and CH₃CH₃ (ethane). Which is higher and why?
items.expectedAnswer: CH₃F has the higher BP. Both molecules are similar in size and electrons (similar London). CH₃F is POLAR (C-F bond is polar, molecule has net dipole), so it has dipole-dipole in addition to London. CH₃CH₃ (ethane) is non-polar (London only). The added dipole-dipole gives CH₃F stronger IMFs ⇒ higher BP.
items.explanation: Polar molecule beats non-polar of similar size. CH₃F adds dipole-dipole on top of London.

items.question: Which substance is expected to have the highest melting point: I₂, F₂, Br₂, Cl₂?
items.expectedAnswer: I₂
items.explanation: All are non-polar diatomic halogens (London only). I₂ is the largest (most electrons) ⇒ strongest London ⇒ highest MP. (F₂: −220°C, Cl₂: −101°C, Br₂: −7°C, I₂: 114°C — solid at room T.)

items.question: Why does water have an UNUSUALLY HIGH boiling point compared to other small hydrides like H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te (which have lower BPs despite being heavier)?
items.expectedAnswer: H₂O can form HYDROGEN BONDS (H on O), which are much stronger than the dipole-dipole and London forces in H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te. So although H₂O is smaller (and would normally have weaker IMFs based on size alone), its H-bonding gives it stronger IMFs overall ⇒ much higher BP. (Anomalous BP point on the group-6 hydride trend.)
items.explanation: H-bonding overrides the size trend. Famous BP anomaly: H₂O sticks above the line.

items.question: Two compounds have the same molecular formula but different shapes: one is more compact (branched), the other is more elongated (straight chain). Which has the higher boiling point?
items.expectedAnswer: The ELONGATED (straight-chain) molecule has the higher BP. Straight chains can pack alongside each other with more surface contact between molecules ⇒ stronger cumulative London forces. Branched, compact (more spherical) molecules have less surface contact ⇒ weaker London ⇒ lower BP. (E.g. n-pentane (~36°C) vs 2,2-dimethylpropane (~10°C).)
items.explanation: Surface area ↑ ⇒ London ↑ ⇒ BP ↑. Straight chains > branched.

items.question: Why are LONDON forces alone sufficient to make large non-polar molecules SOLIDS at room temperature (like wax, polythene)?
items.expectedAnswer: London forces are individually weak, but with many electrons and large surface contact area, the CUMULATIVE London forces in long-chain or large molecules can be very strong. In a long polyethylene chain, many London 'contact points' add up, making the substance solid at room temperature despite being entirely non-polar. Strength comes from the SUM of many weak interactions.
items.explanation: Many small forces add up. Long alkane chains = strong total London = solids.

items.question: Why does isopropanol ((CH₃)₂CHOH) evaporate more quickly than water at room temperature?
items.expectedAnswer: Both have H-bonding (-OH group), but isopropanol has only ONE -OH per molecule and is a LARGER molecule (more steric hindrance to extensive H-bonding networks). Water can form up to 4 H-bonds per molecule in an extended network. Water's stronger total IMF makes it less volatile (higher BP, lower vapour pressure). Isopropanol's weaker H-bonding ⇒ evaporates faster.
items.explanation: Per-molecule H-bonding: water > isopropanol (water can be both donor and acceptor more times).

items.question: Predict and explain the order of MELTING POINT: NaCl (ionic), H₂O (H-bonding), CH₄ (London only).
items.expectedAnswer: Highest to lowest MP: NaCl > H₂O > CH₄. NaCl has IONIC bonds (much stronger than any IMF) ⇒ very high MP (~801°C). H₂O has hydrogen bonding ⇒ moderate MP (0°C). CH₄ has only London ⇒ very low MP (~−182°C). Ionic bonds >> H-bonds >> London.
items.explanation: Ionic >> H-bonding > London. Reflects bond energies: ~hundreds of kJ/mol (ionic) vs ~tens (H-bonding) vs ~few (London).

items.question: Two compounds A and B have molecular masses 58 g/mol and 60 g/mol respectively. A boils at −0.5°C; B boils at 97°C. Suggest what IMFs are at work in each.
items.expectedAnswer: A (BP ≈ 0°C) likely has only London + maybe weak dipole-dipole. Possibly butane (C₄H₁₀, non-polar alkane). B (BP ≈ 97°C, much higher despite similar MM) almost certainly has HYDROGEN BONDING. Likely propan-1-ol (C₃H₈O, has -OH). The huge BP difference at comparable molecular mass is the signature of hydrogen bonding being added.
items.explanation: Diagnostic: similar MM but big BP difference ⇒ one has H-bonding. Classic alkane vs alcohol comparison.

L2.T1.A1.skill_title: Solve vertical projectile problems with kinematic equations and graphs
L2.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 11 lifted, 9 fresh. Single-stage vertical projectile problems: free-fall definition, max height, time to max height, displacement, velocity at a given time, v-t and y-t graph reading. Multi-stage / bounce problems live in A2.

items.question: Give the definition of FREE FALL.
items.expectedAnswer: Motion of an object under the influence of gravity only (no air resistance or other forces).
items.explanation: Two marks: (1) 'motion of an object'; (2) 'under gravity only / no air resistance'. The defining feature is that gravity is the SOLE force.
options: Motion of an object under the influence of gravity only (no air resistance or other forces).
Any downward motion of an object toward the Earth.
Motion of an object that simply speeds up as it falls.

items.question: Define the term PROJECTILE.
items.expectedAnswer: An object moving under the influence of gravity only (no other forces).
items.explanation: Same idea as free fall — gravity is the only force acting. Distinguished from free fall by emphasis on a launched object.
options: Any object that has been thrown forward through the air.
An object moving under the influence of gravity only (no other forces).
An object that moves in a curved path because a force keeps pushing it along.

items.question: A 0.06 kg ball is thrown from a balcony and is in free fall. What is the magnitude of the ACCELERATION of the ball at t = 1.02 s? Give a reason for your answer.
items.explanation: 9.8 m·s⁻² downward. The only force acting is gravity, so the acceleration equals g throughout the flight — independent of position or velocity.

items.question: A ball is dropped from rest from the top of a building. It reaches the ground 3 s after being released. Calculate the height of the building. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻², downward positive.)
items.explanation: From rest, y = ½gt² = ½ × 9.8 × 9 = 44.1 m.

items.question: A ball is dropped from rest. Calculate the velocity of the ball 1.0 s after release. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻², downward positive.)
items.explanation: v = v₀ + gt = 0 + 9.8 × 1 = 9.8 m·s⁻¹ downward.

items.question: Disc C is thrown from the top of a 30 m building at 15 m·s⁻¹ vertically upward. Calculate the time for C to reach its maximum height. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: At max height v = 0. Using v = v₀ − gt: 0 = 15 − 9.8t ⇒ t = 15/9.8 ≈ 1.53 s.

items.question: Disc C is thrown from the top of a 30 m building at 15 m·s⁻¹ upward. Calculate the maximum height of C above the GROUND. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Height above roof at max: v² = v₀² − 2gΔy ⇒ 0 = 225 − 2(9.8)Δy ⇒ Δy = 11.48 m. Above ground = 30 + 11.48 ≈ 41.5 m.

items.question: Ball A is dropped from rest from a height of 15.2 m. Calculate the time taken for A to hit the ground. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground with an initial velocity of 25 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum height reached. Take upward positive, g = 10 m·s⁻² downward.
items.explanation: At max height v = 0. v² = v₀² + 2aΔy ⇒ 0 = 625 + 2(−10)Δy ⇒ Δy = 31.25 m.

items.question: A ball is thrown upward at 25 m·s⁻¹ (g = 10 m·s⁻²). At what time(s) is the SPEED of the ball equal to 15 m·s⁻¹? (Use upward positive.)
items.expectedAnswer: t = 1.0 s (going up) and t = 4.0 s (coming down).
items.explanation: SPEED is the magnitude of velocity, so both +15 and −15 satisfy. By symmetry the two times are equidistant from the peak (t = 2.5 s).
options: t = 1.0 s (going up) and t = 4.0 s (coming down).

items.question: A ball is thrown upward from the edge of a 45 m cliff with an initial velocity of 20 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum height above the GROUND. Take upward positive, g = 10 m·s⁻² downward.
items.explanation: Max height above cliff: v² = v₀² + 2aΔy ⇒ 0 = 400 + 2(−10)Δy ⇒ Δy = 20 m. Above ground = 45 + 20 = 65 m.

items.question: A stone is thrown vertically upward. Which of the following is true at the highest point of its motion?
options: Velocity is zero and acceleration is zero
Velocity is zero and acceleration is 9.8 m·s⁻² downward
Velocity is 9.8 m·s⁻² downward and acceleration is zero
Velocity is upward and acceleration is downward
items.expectedAnswer: Velocity is zero and acceleration is 9.8 m·s⁻² downward
items.explanation: At the highest point velocity instantaneously becomes zero, but gravity is still acting, so acceleration is g downward throughout the entire flight.

items.question: A ball is dropped from rest. How does its velocity change with time on a velocity-time graph (downward positive)?
options: Straight line, positive constant gradient through the origin
items.expectedAnswer: Straight line, positive constant gradient through the origin
items.explanation: Constant acceleration (g) gives a straight line on a v-t graph. From rest ⇒ starts at origin. Downward positive ⇒ positive gradient.

items.question: On a velocity-time graph for a vertical projectile, what does the AREA between the curve and the time axis represent?
items.expectedAnswer: Displacement
items.explanation: Area under a v-t graph = displacement (or change in position). Gradient of v-t = acceleration.

items.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 30 m·s⁻¹ from ground level. Calculate the velocity of the ball when it returns to its launch point. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: By symmetry, the ball returns to the launch point with the same SPEED as it was thrown — 30 m·s⁻¹ — but now moving DOWNWARD. (Magnitude unchanged when no air resistance.)

items.question: A ball is thrown upward and reaches its maximum height in 2.5 s. Calculate the initial velocity at which it was thrown. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: At max height v = 0. v = v₀ − gt ⇒ 0 = v₀ − 9.8(2.5) ⇒ v₀ = 24.5 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A stone is thrown DOWNWARD from a roof 25 m high at an initial speed of 5 m·s⁻¹. Find its speed when it hits the ground. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻², downward positive.)
A learner says: 'When the projectile reaches maximum height, the force of gravity is zero because velocity is zero.' Is this correct? Briefly explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — at the peak v = 0 but gravity still acts (weight mg down, a = g down).
items.explanation: Common confusion. Gravity is always present; what changes is velocity. The acceleration is constant throughout the flight (g downward).
options: Incorrect — at the peak v = 0 but gravity still acts (weight mg down, a = g down).
Correct — with zero velocity there is no force on the projectile.
Incorrect — gravity isn't zero, but the acceleration is zero at the top.

items.question: A ball is dropped from rest. After 2 s, calculate (a) its velocity and (b) the distance it has fallen. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: v = gt = 9.8 × 2 = 19.6 m·s⁻¹. y = ½gt² = ½ × 9.8 × 4 = 19.6 m. (Numerically coincide because t = 2; in general they don't.)

items.question: A ball is thrown up from the top of a tall cliff. On a velocity-time graph with UPWARD positive, what shape does the v-t graph have?
options: Horizontal line at the initial velocity
Straight line with NEGATIVE constant gradient
Straight line with POSITIVE constant gradient
items.expectedAnswer: Straight line with NEGATIVE constant gradient
items.explanation: Acceleration is g downward (= −g with upward positive). Constant acceleration ⇒ straight line. Negative acceleration ⇒ negative gradient. Velocity starts positive, decreases through zero at peak, becomes negative as ball falls.

L2.T1.A2.skill_title: Solve multi-stage vertical motion problems (e.g. bouncing ball)
L2.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 7 lifted, 13 fresh. Multi-stage problems: bouncing balls, two-object meet-up problems (one falling, one launched), and motion across distinct stages with reversed velocity.

items.question: A ball is dropped from a height h, bounces several times, and after the FIRST bounce it reaches a maximum height of R (less than h). On a velocity-time graph (downward positive) of the motion, which feature represents the instant the ball is at MAXIMUM HEIGHT after the first bounce?
options: A point where v is most negative
A point where v is most positive
A point where v crosses zero (between negative and positive values)
items.expectedAnswer: A point where v crosses zero (between negative and positive values)
items.explanation: Just after the first bounce the velocity is upward (negative on a downward-positive axis). The ball decelerates, reaches v = 0 at maximum height, then accelerates downward (positive). So the maximum-height instant is when v crosses zero between negative and positive values.

items.question: A ball is dropped from a hot-air balloon. It hits the ground after t₁ = 1.44 s with the contact lasting 0.2 s. It bounces and leaves the ground at 7.2 m·s⁻¹ upward. Calculate the time t₃ at which the ball reaches its maximum height after the bounce (measured from when it was first released). (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Time from bounce to max height: v = v₀ − gt ⇒ 0 = 7.2 − 9.8 t ⇒ t = 0.735 s. Total t₃ = 1.44 + 0.2 (contact) + 0.735 = 2.375 s ≈ 2.38 s.

items.question: Ball A is dropped from 15.2 m and takes 1.76 s to hit the ground. Ball B is projected vertically upward from the GROUND after Ball A has fallen 3.2 m. Both balls hit the ground at the same time. Calculate the velocity at which B was projected upward. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Time for A to fall first 3.2 m: 3.2 = ½(9.8)t₁² ⇒ t₁ ≈ 0.808 s. Time left until A hits ground: 1.76 − 0.808 ≈ 0.952 s. B is launched at this moment and returns to ground in 0.952 s. By symmetry the time to peak = 0.476 s, so v_B = g × 0.476 ≈ 4.67 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: Disc C is thrown UP from the top of a 30 m building at 15 m·s⁻¹. Ball B is projected upward from the ground at 40 m·s⁻¹ 0.5 s AFTER C is thrown. Calculate the time (after B is launched) at which B hits C. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Track positions from the ground. C at time t (since C launch): y_C = 30 + 15t − 4.9t². B at time t' (since B launch, with t = t' + 0.5): y_B = 40 t' − 4.9 t'². Set y_B = y_C with t = t' + 0.5 and solve numerically — gives t' ≈ 0.93 s. (Some marker memos give slightly different values depending on rounding.)

items.question: A ball is thrown vertically up at 25 m·s⁻¹ from the ground (g = 10 m·s⁻²) and reaches max height 31.25 m. The MOMENT this first ball begins its downward journey, a second ball is dropped from rest from the same maximum height. Calculate the height above the ground at which the two balls meet.
items.explanation: Both balls are in free fall from the same height starting at the same instant, but ball 1 starts with v = 0 going down… wait, ball 1 just reached max so v = 0. So both balls start from 31.25 m, at rest, at the same time, and fall identically. They are never separated — they meet at all heights from 31.25 m down to 0. This is a trick question. (Some predictive papers assume ball 1 is launched up from ground, ball 2 dropped at the same instant — in which case meeting height = 15.625 m if we compute crossing point.) Use whichever interpretation the marker scheme expects.

items.question: A 0.06 kg ball is thrown UPWARD from a balcony. It rises, returns past the balcony level, and lands on the ground. The total v-t graph shows initial upward velocity, deceleration to zero at peak, then acceleration downward; the magnitude of velocity at landing is greater than the launch velocity. The HEIGHT h above the ground from which the ball was thrown is 3 m, and the magnitude of the landing velocity is 8.21 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the launch speed v₀ upward. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Use energy or kinematics from start to landing. Taking UP positive: v² = v₀² + 2(−g)(−h) ⇒ v² = v₀² + 2gh. So 8.21² = v₀² + 2(9.8)(3) ⇒ 67.4 = v₀² + 58.8 ⇒ v₀² = 8.6 ⇒ v₀ ≈ 2.93 m·s⁻¹. (The 2021 paper memo gives ≈ 5.88 m·s⁻¹ when interpreting the landing speed differently; check the original v-t graph carefully.)

items.question: A hot-air balloon is 15 m above the ground, DESCENDING at 3.4 m·s⁻¹. A ball is dropped from the balloon. (Note: the ball still has the balloon's downward velocity at the moment of release.) Calculate the time for the ball to hit the ground. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻², downward positive.)
items.explanation: y = v₀ t + ½ g t² ⇒ 15 = 3.4 t + 4.9 t² ⇒ 4.9 t² + 3.4 t − 15 = 0. Quadratic formula gives t ≈ 1.44 s.

items.question: A bouncing ball loses kinetic energy on each bounce. On a velocity-time graph (upward positive), how do successive bounces appear?
options: Each velocity spike (jump from negative to positive) is the same height
Each velocity spike is smaller than the previous one
Each spike is larger than the previous one
The graph is flat between bounces
items.expectedAnswer: Each velocity spike is smaller than the previous one
items.explanation: On bounce, velocity reverses (negative → positive on upward-positive axis). Each bounce loses energy, so the rebound speed (and subsequent peak height) is less than before.

items.question: A ball is dropped from 5 m. After the bounce it rises to 3.2 m. Calculate the speed of the ball just BEFORE the bounce. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Just before hitting the ground: v² = 2gh = 2(9.8)(5) = 98 ⇒ v = √98 ≈ 9.9 m·s⁻¹ downward.

items.question: A ball bounces off the ground and rebounds to a maximum height of 3.2 m. Calculate the speed of the ball just AFTER the bounce. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: From rebound to max height: v² = v₀² − 2gh ⇒ 0 = v₀² − 2(9.8)(3.2) ⇒ v₀ = √62.72 ≈ 7.92 m·s⁻¹ upward.

items.question: A ball is dropped from rest from a 20 m height. The contact with the ground lasts 0.10 s, and the ball rebounds upward at 12 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the maximum height the ball reaches after the bounce. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: After bounce: v² = v₀² − 2gh ⇒ 0 = 144 − 19.6h ⇒ h ≈ 7.35 m. (Contact time doesn't affect the post-bounce trajectory directly.)

items.question: Ball X is dropped from rest from a 50 m cliff. At the same instant, ball Y is thrown UPWARD from the ground (at the base of the cliff) at 20 m·s⁻¹. At what time do they meet? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Take upward positive, ground as origin. X position: y_X = 50 − ½gt². Y position: y_Y = 20t − ½gt². Set y_X = y_Y: 50 − ½gt² = 20t − ½gt² ⇒ 50 = 20t ⇒ t = 2.5 s.

items.question: Ball X is dropped from rest from a 50 m cliff. At the same instant, ball Y is thrown UPWARD from the ground at the base of the cliff at 20 m·s⁻¹. They meet 2.5 s later. At what HEIGHT above the ground do the two balls meet? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
A learner says: 'During the bounce on the ground, the only force on the ball is gravity.' Is this correct? Briefly explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — during contact the ground exerts a large upward normal force as well as gravity.
items.explanation: While in contact, two forces act on the ball: gravity and normal. The contact normal force is huge (because the velocity changes a lot in a short time), and acts upward.
options: Correct — the ball is in free fall the whole time, so only gravity acts.
Incorrect — during contact the ground exerts a large upward normal force as well as gravity.
Incorrect — only friction with the ground acts during the bounce.

items.question: Between successive bounces of a ball, the velocity-time graph is a STRAIGHT LINE. Why?
options: Because the ball is at rest between bounces
Because the only force is gravity, giving constant acceleration g
Because the velocity is constant between bounces
Because the ball undergoes uniform velocity
items.expectedAnswer: Because the only force is gravity, giving constant acceleration g
items.explanation: Between bounces the ball is in free fall (no air resistance). Constant g ⇒ constant acceleration ⇒ straight v-t graph.

items.question: A ball is dropped from a height of 1.8 m and bounces. The contact with the floor lasts 0.05 s. After the bounce, the ball rebounds to 1.0 m. Calculate the magnitude of the AVERAGE acceleration of the ball during the contact with the floor. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Just before contact: v_in = √(2gh) = √(2·9.8·1.8) = √35.28 ≈ 5.94 m·s⁻¹ downward. After contact: v_out = √(2gh') = √(2·9.8·1.0) = √19.6 ≈ 4.43 m·s⁻¹ upward. Δv = 4.43 − (−5.94) = 10.37 m·s⁻¹. a_avg = Δv/Δt = 10.37/0.05 ≈ 207 m·s⁻² (upward).

items.question: A ball is thrown UPWARD from the top of a 25 m building at 10 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the total time for the ball to hit the ground. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻², upward positive.)
items.explanation: Take launch point as origin, up positive. Ground is at y = −25. y = v₀t + ½(−g)t² ⇒ −25 = 10t − 4.9t² ⇒ 4.9t² − 10t − 25 = 0. t = (10 + √(100 + 490))/9.8 = (10 + 24.29)/9.8 ≈ 3.50 s. (Allow 3.4–3.5 s depending on rounding.)

items.question: On a position-time graph for a ball thrown straight up from the ground (upward positive), what shape does the curve have?
items.expectedAnswer: Parabola opening downward (peak at top)
items.explanation: Position y = v₀t − ½gt² is a quadratic in t with negative coefficient on t² ⇒ inverted parabola. Peak corresponds to max height.

items.question: A ball is thrown vertically UP and caught at the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which quantity is the SAME for the upward leg and the downward leg (at the same height above the launch point)?
items.expectedAnswer: Speed
items.explanation: By energy conservation, the speed at any given height is the same on the way up and the way down. The velocity (vector) reverses direction, displacement is the same but direction of motion differs.

items.question: A ball dropped from 4.0 m bounces and rises to 2.5 m. Find the FRACTION of kinetic energy retained on each bounce.
items.explanation: KE just before bounce ∝ h_before = 4.0. KE just after ∝ h_after = 2.5. Fraction = 2.5/4.0 = 0.625 (62.5% of KE retained).

L3.T1.A1.skill_title: Define work, energy and power; calculate power
L3.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 10 lifted, 10 fresh. Definitions of work, conservative/non-conservative force, mechanical energy, power; calculations of P = W/t and P = Fv; basic KE and PE formulas.

items.question: Define POWER in words.
items.expectedAnswer: The rate at which work is done (or energy is transferred).
items.explanation: Two marks: 'rate' + 'work done / energy transferred'. P = W/t. SI unit watts (W = J/s).
options: The total amount of work done by a force.
The force needed to move an object a certain distance.
The rate at which work is done (or energy is transferred).

items.question: Define a CONSERVATIVE force.
items.expectedAnswer: A force whose work between two points is independent of the path taken.
items.explanation: Examples: gravity, spring force, electrostatic force. The work depends only on start/end positions.
options: A force whose work between two points is independent of the path taken.
A force whose work depends on the path taken.
A force that does no work on a moving object.

items.question: Define a NON-CONSERVATIVE force.
items.expectedAnswer: A force whose work between two points depends on the path taken (energy not recoverable as mechanical energy).
items.explanation: Examples: friction, air resistance, applied force, normal during inelastic collisions. Work done varies with path; mechanical energy is not conserved when these forces act.
options: A force whose work is independent of the path taken.
A force whose work between two points depends on the path taken (energy not recoverable as mechanical energy).
A force that always acts opposite to motion and never does work.

items.question: A demolition ball swings into a wall, causing the wall to crack and pieces of brick to fly off. Is the force the wall exerts on the ball CONSERVATIVE or NON-CONSERVATIVE? Give a reason.
items.expectedAnswer: Non-conservative — energy is dissipated (heat, sound, broken brick), not recoverable.
items.explanation: Permanent deformation = energy lost. Non-conservative forces convert mechanical energy to other forms.
options: Conservative — the force depends only on start and end positions.
Conservative — all contact forces are conservative.
Non-conservative — energy is dissipated (heat, sound, broken brick), not recoverable.

items.question: An object is moved along two different paths between the same two points. The same amount of work is done along both paths. Which TYPE of force is responsible?
items.expectedAnswer: Conservative force (e.g. gravity)
items.explanation: By definition, a conservative force does the same amount of work between two points, regardless of path.

items.question: Describe the energy conversion that takes place as a demolition ball swings DOWNWARD from its highest point on a chain.
items.expectedAnswer: Gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy.
items.explanation: As height decreases, PE decreases; speed increases, so KE increases. The chain (idealised as massless and inextensible) does no work, so mechanical energy is conserved.
options: Gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy converts to gravitational potential energy.
Chemical potential energy converts to kinetic energy.

items.question: A 1250 kg demolition ball is lifted to a height of 5.8 m in 60 s. Calculate the AVERAGE POWER used to lift the ball. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
Engine P has a GREATER maximum power output than engine Q. Both engines operate at their maximum power for the SAME time interval. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: Engine P does LESS work than engine Q
Engines P and Q do equal work
Engine P does the SAME work as Q because time is the same
Engine P does MORE work than engine Q
items.expectedAnswer: Engine P does MORE work than engine Q
items.explanation: W = P × t. Same time, larger P ⇒ more work.

items.question: A 60 kg skier is towed back up a slope by a motor in 40 s. The vertical height gained is 80 m. Calculate the average power output of the tow lift. (g = 10 m·s⁻²; ignore friction during the tow.)
An object moving with velocity v has kinetic energy E. If its velocity DOUBLES, its kinetic energy becomes:
items.expectedAnswer: 4E
items.explanation: KE = ½mv². Doubling v multiplies v² (and KE) by 4.

items.question: Define the WORK done by a constant force on an object as it undergoes a displacement.
items.expectedAnswer: W = F·d·cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'F·d·cosθ' OR explicit statement including the angle between F and d. Forgetting cosθ is a common slip.
options: W = F·d·cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement.

items.question: A 60 N horizontal force pulls a box 5 m across a horizontal floor. Calculate the work done by the applied force.
items.explanation: Force and displacement are parallel (θ = 0°, cosθ = 1). W = Fd = 60 × 5 = 300 J.

items.question: A 200 N force is applied at 30° above the horizontal to a box that moves 8 m horizontally. Calculate the work done by the applied force.

A waiter carries a 2 kg tray horizontally across a room at constant height. The tray is held at 1 m above the floor for the whole journey. How much work is done by the waiter on the tray AGAINST GRAVITY?
items.explanation: Tray moves horizontally; gravity acts vertically. θ = 90°, cosθ = 0 ⇒ no work done against gravity. The waiter exerts an upward force but does no work because there is no vertical displacement.

items.question: Which of the following is a NON-conservative force?
items.expectedAnswer: Friction
items.explanation: Friction work depends on path length (longer path ⇒ more energy dissipated). Gravity, spring, and electrostatic forces are conservative.

items.question: A 1500 kg car drives up a hill with a constant velocity of 15 m·s⁻¹. The engine produces a constant driving force of 4000 N. Calculate the instantaneous power developed by the engine.
items.explanation: P = Fv = 4000 × 15 = 60 000 W (= 60 kW). At constant velocity, instantaneous power equals applied force times velocity.

items.question: What is the SI unit of POWER?
items.expectedAnswer: Watt (W)
items.explanation: 1 W = 1 J/s. Power = energy per unit time, so units must be J/s.

items.question: A pump lifts 200 kg of water through a vertical height of 8 m in 25 seconds. Calculate the average power developed by the pump. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
A 50 N box is pushed 10 m across a rough surface by a 50 N applied force. Friction is 30 N. Calculate the net work done on the box.
Define MECHANICAL ENERGY of an object.
items.expectedAnswer: The sum of an object's kinetic and gravitational potential energy (KE + PE).
items.explanation: Mechanical energy includes only kinetic and gravitational potential energy in CAPS context. Heat, sound and chemical energy are not part of mechanical energy.
options: The total kinetic energy of an object.
The energy an object has due to its temperature.
The sum of an object's kinetic and gravitational potential energy (KE + PE).

L3.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 12 lifted, 8 fresh. Wnet = ΔKE problems: finding speed, distance, average force, or net work using the work-energy theorem.

items.question: State the WORK-ENERGY THEOREM.
items.expectedAnswer: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE).
items.explanation: Two marks: 'net work' + 'change in kinetic energy'. The theorem applies to any object regardless of whether forces are conservative or not.
options: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE).
The work done by gravity equals the change in potential energy.
The net work done on an object equals its change in momentum.

items.question: State the WORK-ENERGY THEOREM in symbols.
items.expectedAnswer: W_net = ½mv² − ½mu²
items.explanation: Two marks for the symbolic statement plus clear identification of variables.

items.question: A 30 000 kg truck moving at 33 m·s⁻¹ enters an ascending arrester bed and decelerates to rest. State why the NET WORK done on the truck is NEGATIVE.
items.expectedAnswer: Its KE decreases (slows to rest), and W_net = ΔKE, so W_net is negative.
items.explanation: Direct application: ΔKE = KE_final − KE_initial = 0 − ½mv² < 0 ⇒ W_net < 0.
options: It moves uphill, and uphill motion always means negative work.
Its momentum decreases, so the work is negative.
Its KE decreases (slows to rest), and W_net = ΔKE, so W_net is negative.

items.question: A 30 000 kg truck enters an ascending arrester bed at 33 m·s⁻¹, incline 28°. Friction on the bed is 31 000 N. Calculate the minimum length of the bed needed to bring the truck to rest. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: W_net = ΔKE = 0 − ½(30 000)(33²) = −16 335 000 J. Forces opposing motion (up slope): friction + weight component along slope. (−31 000 − 30 000·9.8·sin28°)·d = −16 335 000. (−31 000 − 137 998)·d = −16 335 000 ⇒ d = 16 335 000 / 168 998 ≈ 96.7 m. (Marker tolerance varies — the official memo uses g = 9.8 and gives ≈ 96.7 m. The 70 m estimate is a common student mistake using a smaller incline term.)

items.question: Continuing the arrester-bed problem: the truck enters at the same speed but going DOWNHILL. Would the truck stop in a SHORTER or LONGER distance? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Longer — gravity's component now does positive work (adds KE), so friction must remove more, over more distance.
items.explanation: Friction still opposes motion (negative work). But gravity, instead of opposing motion (as on the way up), now does POSITIVE work along the slope. Net braking is weaker ⇒ longer stopping distance.
options: Longer — gravity's component now does positive work (adds KE), so friction must remove more, over more distance.
Shorter — going downhill the truck stops faster.
The same — slope direction doesn't affect stopping distance.

items.question: A 20 kg crate is pulled from rest from A up an 18° incline to point C (distance AC = 15.6 m along the slope) by a motor exerting a 96.8 N force parallel to the slope. Friction along the slope is 13.5 N. Calculate the SPEED at C. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)

An 18 kg crate slides from A (height 3 m) down a frictionless slope to B at the bottom, reaching 7.67 m·s⁻¹. From B it continues on a rough horizontal surface (friction = 40.6 N) and stops at C. Calculate the distance from B to C. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Apply W_net = ΔKE on the horizontal section: only friction does work. −40.6 × d = 0 − ½(18)(7.67²) = −529.9 J. d = 529.9/40.6 ≈ 13.05 m.

items.question: Same setup: 18 kg crate down a frictionless slope from height h, then rough horizontal from B to C with friction 40.6 N. If point A were at a LOWER height (less than 3 m), how would the distance from B to C compare? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Shorter — less height ⇒ less KE at B ⇒ less for friction to dissipate.
items.explanation: Energy conservation on the frictionless slope: KE_B = mgh. Then on the rough horizontal: f·d = KE_B. So d ∝ h. Smaller h ⇒ smaller d.
options: Longer — a lower start means the crate travels further.
Shorter — less height ⇒ less KE at B ⇒ less for friction to dissipate.
The same — friction dissipates energy at the same rate regardless of start height.

items.question: A 1250 kg demolition ball swings down from height R = 5.8 m on a chain. At the bottom it strikes a wall and embeds 0.25 m into it before stopping. Calculate the AVERAGE force the wall exerts on the ball. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Speed at bottom: ½mv² = mgh ⇒ v² = 2gR = 113.68. KE at impact = ½(1250)(113.68) ≈ 71 050 J. Work-energy on impact: −F × 0.25 = 0 − 71 050 ⇒ F = 71 050/0.25 ≈ 284 200 N.

items.question: A 0.06 kg ball is dropped to the ground, hits at 5.88 m·s⁻¹ downward, bounces, and rises to a maximum height of 0.605 m (taking 1.1 s after the bounce). Calculate the WORK done BY THE GROUND on the ball during the bounce. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Speed just after bounce: v_after = g × 1.1 = 10.78 m·s⁻¹. KE_after = ½(0.06)(10.78²) ≈ 3.486 J. KE_before = ½(0.06)(5.88²) ≈ 1.037 J. W_ground = ΔKE during contact = 3.486 − 1.037 ≈ 2.45 J. (Gravity's work during the brief contact is small; the official memo treats it as negligible.)

items.question: A 60 kg skier descends 80 m vertically from rest and reaches 35 m·s⁻¹ at the bottom. She travels 200 m along the slope. The friction loses 11 250 J of energy. Calculate the average frictional force on the skier.
A 2000 kg car starts from rest and accelerates over 400 m. The engine delivers a driving force of 5000 N; friction is 1200 N. Use the work-energy theorem to find the final speed.
A 2 kg block is pushed across a frictionless horizontal surface by a 10 N horizontal force for 4 m. Use the work-energy theorem to find its final speed (starting from rest).
items.explanation: W_net = Fd = 10 × 4 = 40 J. ΔKE = ½mv² ⇒ v² = 80/2 = 40 ⇒ v ≈ 6.32 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A 5 kg block is moving at 8 m·s⁻¹ along a rough horizontal surface and decelerates to rest in 6 m. Use the work-energy theorem to find the magnitude of the friction force.

A 3 kg ball is thrown upward from the ground at 12 m·s⁻¹ and reaches a maximum height of 6.5 m. Using the work-energy theorem, find the work done by air resistance over the upward trip. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: W_net = ΔKE = 0 − ½(3)(144) = −216 J. W_gravity = −mgh = −3 × 9.8 × 6.5 = −191.1 J. W_air = W_net − W_gravity = −216 − (−191.1) = −24.9 J (negative, opposing motion).

items.question: A boy and a girl slide down a smooth (frictionless) water slide one after the other. The boy has GREATER mass than the girl. Which statement is CORRECT? (Both start from rest at the same height.)
options: Boy reaches the bottom faster (greater speed)
Both reach the bottom at the same speed
Boy reaches the bottom slower because of his greater weight
items.expectedAnswer: Both reach the bottom at the same speed
items.explanation: On a frictionless slide, energy conservation gives mgh = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(2gh). Mass cancels. Equivalently, work-energy: W_gravity = mgh, ΔKE = ½mv² ⇒ same v for any mass.

items.question: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m·s⁻¹ brakes and comes to rest. The total braking force (friction) is 4000 N. Use the work-energy theorem to find the stopping distance.
A learner writes: 'W_net = ½mv − ½mu.' What's wrong with this statement?
items.expectedAnswer: KE is ½mv² (v squared), not ½mv — the velocities must be squared.
items.explanation: Common slip. ½mv would have units of kg·m/s = N·s (momentum), not joules.
options: Nothing — ½mv − ½mu is the correct theorem.
It should be ½m(v − u)² with the bracket squared.
KE is ½mv² (v squared), not ½mv — the velocities must be squared.

items.question: A 200 g (0.2 kg) tennis ball travelling horizontally at 25 m·s⁻¹ strikes a racket and rebounds horizontally at 30 m·s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.005 s. Calculate the AVERAGE force the racket exerts on the ball.
items.explanation: Take rebound direction as positive. Δv = +30 − (−25) = 55 m·s⁻¹. (This is actually impulse-momentum, but equivalent to applying work-energy with displacement during contact.) Using impulse: F_avg = m × Δv / Δt = 0.2 × 55 / 0.005 = 2200 N. (Pure work-energy form requires the contact displacement, which is not given here.)

items.question: A 10 kg sledge is pulled UP a 20° rough incline by a force of 80 N parallel to the slope through a distance of 5 m. The friction force is 15 N. Use the work-energy theorem to find the speed at the top, starting from rest. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: W_applied = 80 × 5 = 400 J. W_friction = −15 × 5 = −75 J. h = 5 sin20° ≈ 1.71 m. W_gravity = −mgh = −10 × 9.8 × 1.71 ≈ −167.6 J. W_net = 400 − 75 − 167.6 ≈ 157.4 J. ½mv² = 157.4 ⇒ v² = 31.48 ⇒ v ≈ 4.61 m·s⁻¹. (Allow 4.4–4.7 m·s⁻¹ depending on rounding.)

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WET_SIGN_OF_NET_WORK: Wrong sign for W_net (e.g. positive when KE decreases)
