L3.T1.A3.notes: 20 items: 6 lifted, 14 fresh. Conservation of mechanical energy on frictionless surfaces; identifying when the principle applies (and when it doesn't).

items.question: State the principle of CONSERVATION OF MECHANICAL ENERGY.
items.expectedAnswer: Total mechanical energy stays constant when only conservative forces do work on the system.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'total mechanical energy' + 'conservative forces only / no non-conservative work'. If friction or other non-conservative forces act, mechanical energy is NOT conserved.
options: Total mechanical energy stays constant when only conservative forces do work on the system.
Total mechanical energy stays constant in all situations.
Energy is always created and destroyed in equal amounts.

items.question: An 18 kg crate slides from rest down a FRICTIONLESS slope through a vertical height of 3 m. Calculate the speed at the bottom. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Frictionless ⇒ mechanical energy conserved. mgh = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 3) = √58.8 ≈ 7.67 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A hot-air balloon descends at CONSTANT SPEED. Which statement about its GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL ENERGY is CORRECT?
items.expectedAnswer: It decreases
items.explanation: PE = mgh. Descending ⇒ h decreases ⇒ PE decreases. (KE stays constant at constant speed; the lost PE is dissipated as work against air resistance / heat — mechanical energy is NOT conserved here because air resistance acts.)

items.question: A stone is dropped from rest from a height h. After it has fallen ¼ of h (i.e. it is now at height ¾h), how does its kinetic energy compare to mgh?
items.expectedAnswer: KE = ¼mgh
items.explanation: Energy conservation: PE_lost = KE_gained. After falling ¼h, the stone lost PE = mg(¼h) = ¼mgh. So KE = ¼mgh.

items.question: A ball falls freely from rest under gravity. Which statement about its KINETIC ENERGY (Ek) and MOMENTUM (p) as it falls is CORRECT?
options: Both Ek and p stay constant
items.expectedAnswer: Both Ek and p increase
items.explanation: As the ball accelerates (gravity), velocity increases. Ek = ½mv² increases. p = mv increases. (Mechanical energy IS conserved: PE → KE.)

items.question: A 60 kg skier starts from rest at the top of an 80 m high slope. At the bottom her speed is 35 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the work done by friction on the skier. (g = 10 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Energy conservation with friction: PE_top = KE_bottom + |W_friction|. PE = mgh = 60 × 10 × 80 = 48 000 J. KE = ½(60)(35²) = 36 750 J. |W_friction| = 48 000 − 36 750 = 11 250 J.

items.question: Under what conditions is mechanical energy conserved?
items.expectedAnswer: When only conservative forces do work (no net work by non-conservative forces like friction).
items.explanation: Friction, applied forces, normal force during inelastic collisions all break conservation. The textbook 'frictionless and no air resistance' is the usual simplification.
options: When only conservative forces do work (no net work by non-conservative forces like friction).
Only when the object moves in a straight line.

items.question: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from rest from 4 m above the ground (no air resistance). Calculate its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: KE_bottom = PE_top = mgh = 0.5 × 9.8 × 4 = 19.6 J.

items.question: A 2 kg pendulum bob is pulled aside until it is 0.3 m above its lowest point, then released. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed at the lowest point. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Tension on a string does no work (perpendicular to motion). Only gravity does work. mgh = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.3) = √5.88 ≈ 2.42 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A 1 kg ball is thrown straight UP from the ground at 8 m·s⁻¹ (no air resistance). Calculate the maximum height it reaches. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: Energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh ⇒ h = v²/(2g) = 64/(19.6) ≈ 3.27 m.

items.question: A learner says: 'Total mechanical energy is conserved when a block slides down a rough incline.' Is this correct? Briefly explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — friction is non-conservative and dissipates energy, so mechanical energy is not conserved.
items.explanation: Conservation of mechanical energy applies only when non-conservative forces do no net work. Friction breaks the assumption.
options: Correct — mechanical energy is always conserved on an incline.
Correct — friction only changes direction, not total energy.
Incorrect — friction is non-conservative and dissipates energy, so mechanical energy is not conserved.

items.question: A 0.3 kg toy car rolls from rest down a frictionless track from height 1.2 m, then through a flat section, then up a smooth hill. What maximum height does it reach on the second hill (in metres)?
items.explanation: Frictionless + only conservative forces ⇒ mechanical energy conserved. Final PE = initial PE ⇒ h_final = h_initial = 1.2 m.

items.question: A 0.05 kg arrow is fired straight UP with an initial speed of 35 m·s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed when it is 50 m above the launch point? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: ½mu² = ½mv² + mgh ⇒ v² = u² − 2gh = 1225 − 2(9.8)(50) = 1225 − 980 = 245 ⇒ v ≈ 15.65 m·s⁻¹. (Allow ~15.6–17.5 m·s⁻¹ depending on rounding of g.)

items.question: An object slides down a frictionless 4 m high ramp. At what height above the bottom does its kinetic energy equal its remaining potential energy?
items.explanation: KE = PE_remaining ⇒ mg(4 − h) = mgh ⇒ h = 2 m. (Halfway down.)

items.question: A 2 kg block is at the top of a frictionless 5 m incline (vertical height 5 m above the bottom). Total mechanical energy at the top, relative to the bottom, is:
items.explanation: At top, at rest: KE = 0, PE = mgh = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 J. Total mechanical energy = 98 J.

items.question: Continuing: same 2 kg block from 5 m high (frictionless). It reaches the bottom. What is its kinetic energy at the bottom, and its speed? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: KE_bottom = PE_top = 98 J. ½mv² = 98 ⇒ v² = 98 ⇒ v ≈ 9.9 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A skateboarder enters a frictionless half-pipe at 8 m·s⁻¹. How high (above the entry level) can the skateboarder rise? (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
Why does the tension in a swinging pendulum string do NO work on the pendulum bob?
items.expectedAnswer: Tension is along the string, perpendicular to the motion (θ = 90°), so W = Fd cos90° = 0.
items.explanation: This is why pendulum problems are great for energy conservation: only gravity does work; tension is always perpendicular to instantaneous motion.
options: Tension is along the string, perpendicular to the motion (θ = 90°), so W = Fd cos90° = 0.
Because the bob has no displacement.

items.question: A 4 kg ball is at the top of a frictionless track at height 2 m, moving at 3 m·s⁻¹ horizontally. Find its speed at the bottom. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
Two identical balls are released from rest from the same height — one falls straight down, the other slides down a frictionless curved ramp. Compare their SPEEDS at ground level.
items.expectedAnswer: Equal — same drop height, only gravity does work, so v = √(2gh) regardless of path.
items.explanation: Path independence of conservative forces. Same start and end heights ⇒ same KE at the bottom ⇒ same speed.
options: The straight-down ball is faster because its path is shorter.
Equal — same drop height, only gravity does work, so v = √(2gh) regardless of path.
The ramp ball is faster because it gains speed along the slope.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_CME_CONDITIONS: Doesn't recognise when conservation applies (e.g. tries to apply with friction)

L4.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply conservation of momentum to collisions and explosions
L4.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 13 lifted, 7 fresh. Conservation of linear momentum applied to elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic collisions, and explosions/separations. Includes elastic-check calculations.

items.question: State the principle of CONSERVATION OF LINEAR MOMENTUM.
items.expectedAnswer: The total linear momentum of an isolated system (no net external force) stays constant.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'total linear momentum' + 'isolated / no net external force'. Without the 'isolated' qualifier, the statement is incomplete.
options: The total linear momentum of any system always stays constant.
Momentum is conserved as long as the objects keep moving.
The total linear momentum of an isolated system (no net external force) stays constant.

items.question: Define the term ISOLATED SYSTEM in the context of momentum.
items.expectedAnswer: A system on which the net external force is zero.
items.explanation: Internal forces between parts of the system can be present (collisions, explosions); only the net EXTERNAL force must be zero.
options: A system on which the net external force is zero.
A system that contains only one object.
A system where no objects touch each other.

items.question: Trolley A collides with stationary trolley B and the two trolleys STICK TOGETHER after the collision. Which statement about this collision is CORRECT?
options: Both kinetic energy and momentum are conserved
Kinetic energy is conserved; momentum is not
Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not
items.expectedAnswer: Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not
items.explanation: Stick together = perfectly inelastic collision. Momentum is always conserved for isolated systems; kinetic energy is NOT conserved in inelastic collisions (some KE → heat, sound, deformation).

items.question: A ball is dropped from a height h and its momentum just before hitting the ground is p. The ball is then dropped from a height of 2h. What is the magnitude of the new momentum just before hitting the ground?
A compressed spring is placed between trolleys P (mass m₁) and Q (mass m₂), initially at rest. When released, Q moves to the RIGHT at velocity v. What is the momentum of trolley P?
items.expectedAnswer: m₂v to the left
items.explanation: Initial total momentum = 0 (both at rest). After release: p_P + p_Q = 0. p_Q = +m₂v (right). So p_P = −m₂v (left).

items.question: Trolley A (7.2 kg) moves at 0.4 m·s⁻¹ towards STATIONARY trolley B (5.3 kg). They collide and LOCK TOGETHER. Calculate the velocity of the combined trolleys after collision.
items.explanation: p_before = 7.2 × 0.4 = 2.88 kg·m·s⁻¹. p_after = (7.2 + 5.3)v = 12.5v. Setting equal: v = 2.88/12.5 ≈ 0.230 m·s⁻¹ in the original direction.

items.question: Trolley A (2 kg) moves right at 0.7 m·s⁻¹ and collides with stationary trolley B (3 kg). After the collision, A moves right at 0.1 m·s⁻¹ and B moves right at v_B. Calculate v_B.

Trolley A (2 kg) moves right at 0.7 m·s⁻¹ and collides with a stationary trolley B (3 kg). After the collision, A moves right at 0.1 m·s⁻¹ and B moves right at 0.4 m·s⁻¹. Was the collision ELASTIC? Show with a calculation.
items.expectedAnswer: Inelastic — KE drops from 0.49 J to 0.25 J, so kinetic energy is not conserved.
items.explanation: Elastic ⇔ KE conserved. Compute KE before and after; compare.
options: Elastic — momentum is conserved, so KE must be too.
Inelastic — KE drops from 0.49 J to 0.25 J, so kinetic energy is not conserved.
Elastic — KE before (0.49 J) equals KE after.

items.question: Trolleys A (3.2 kg) and B (2.6 kg) are held together with a compressed spring (initially at rest). When released, A moves to the LEFT at 0.4 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of B.
Continuing: trolley C has a LARGER mass than B (same spring, same compression, same partner A). How does the velocity of C after release compare to that of B? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Smaller — by conservation of momentum, the larger mass leaves with the smaller velocity.
items.explanation: Same impulse on the other side (because the spring exerts the same impulse) ⇒ same momentum gained ⇒ heavier mass means smaller velocity.
options: Larger — a heavier trolley carries more velocity.
The same — the spring gives every trolley the same velocity.
Smaller — by conservation of momentum, the larger mass leaves with the smaller velocity.

items.question: A rocket is mounted on a cart (combined mass 20 kg) moving at 2.5 m·s⁻¹. The rocket is fired and moves at 30 m·s⁻¹; the (lighter) cart slows to 0.6 m·s⁻¹. Both move in the original direction. Calculate the mass of the rocket.

A 1200 kg car travelling east at 20 m·s⁻¹ collides with an 800 kg car travelling west at 15 m·s⁻¹. After collision the 1200 kg car continues east at 5 m·s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the 800 kg car after the collision (take east positive).
A 4 kg trolley A moving east at 6 m·s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley B. After collision they MOVE TOGETHER. Calculate their common velocity.
items.explanation: m_A·v_A = (m_A + m_B)v_f ⇒ 4·6 = 6·v_f ⇒ v_f = 4 m·s⁻¹ east.

items.question: Same collision: 4 kg trolley at 6 m·s⁻¹ hits stationary 2 kg trolley, stick together at 4 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the kinetic energy LOST during the collision.
items.explanation: KE_before = ½(4)(36) = 72 J. KE_after = ½(6)(16) = 48 J. Lost = 72 − 48 = 24 J.

items.question: Define the LINEAR MOMENTUM of an object.
items.expectedAnswer: The product of mass and velocity (p = mv); a vector, in the direction of the velocity.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'p = mv' + 'vector / direction same as velocity'.
options: The product of mass and velocity (p = mv); a vector, in the direction of the velocity.
The product of mass and velocity; a scalar quantity.
The product of mass and acceleration.

items.question: A 0.5 kg ball moving east at 4 m·s⁻¹ collides head-on with a 0.3 kg ball moving west at 6 m·s⁻¹. After collision the 0.5 kg ball moves west at 1 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of the 0.3 kg ball after collision (east positive).
A 1 kg ball moving east at 4 m·s⁻¹ collides head-on with a 1 kg ball moving west at 4 m·s⁻¹. They stick together. What is the final velocity?
items.explanation: Σp_before = 1(+4) + 1(−4) = 0. After sticking, momentum is still zero, so v = 0.

items.question: A learner says: 'Momentum is conserved in EVERY collision, even if external forces act.' Is this strictly correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Not strictly — only for an isolated system; external forces change total momentum.
items.explanation: Strict statement: isolated system required. In practice, internal collision forces are huge compared to external forces over the short collision time.
options: Correct — momentum is always conserved in any collision.
Not strictly — only for an isolated system; external forces change total momentum.
Correct — collisions are always isolated systems.

items.question: A 0.05 kg bullet is fired into a 2 kg block of wood resting on a frictionless surface. The bullet embeds in the wood and the combined system moves off at 4 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the bullet's initial velocity.
Two ice skaters stand at rest face-to-face on frictionless ice. Skater A (60 kg) pushes off skater B (40 kg). After the push, A moves backward at 2 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the velocity of B.
items.explanation: p_initial = 0. 0 = 60(−2) + 40(v_B) ⇒ v_B = 120/40 = 3 m·s⁻¹ in the opposite direction to A.

L4.T1.A2.skill_title: Calculate impulse and apply the impulse-momentum theorem
L4.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 10 lifted, 10 fresh. Impulse = FΔt = Δp; area under F-t graph; sign conventions on rebounds; safety applications (extending contact time).

items.question: The change in momentum of an object equals:
items.expectedAnswer: The impulse on it
items.explanation: Impulse-momentum theorem: Impulse = FΔt = Δp = m(v − u).

items.question: What physical quantity does the AREA under a force-time graph represent?
items.expectedAnswer: Impulse — the change in momentum (Δp).
items.explanation: Impulse = ∫F dt = area under F-t curve. By the impulse-momentum theorem, this equals Δp.
options: The work done by the force.
The average force on the object.

items.question: A cricket player catches a ball by moving his hands DOWNWARD as he catches it. The main reason for this technique is to:
options: Increase the force exerted on the hands
Increase the contact time and so decrease the force on the hands
items.expectedAnswer: Increase the contact time and so decrease the force on the hands
items.explanation: Δp is fixed (ball comes to rest). Impulse = F·Δt = Δp. Larger Δt ⇒ smaller F. The hands experience less force — safer for the catcher.

items.question: A 0.15 kg cricket ball travelling at 30 m·s⁻¹ horizontally is hit by a bat and rebounds at 40 m·s⁻¹ in the OPPOSITE direction. Calculate the change in momentum of the ball.
items.explanation: Take initial direction as positive. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) = 0.15(−40 − 30) = 0.15(−70) = −10.5 kg·m·s⁻¹. Magnitude 10.5 N·s, directed opposite to the ball's initial motion.

items.question: Continuing: the bat is in contact with the cricket ball for 0.005 s. Calculate the magnitude of the average force exerted by the bat on the ball.

Trolley A (7.2 kg, initially at 0.4 m·s⁻¹) and stationary trolley B (5.3 kg) collide and lock together, moving at 0.23 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the AVERAGE force A exerts on B during the collision if it lasts 0.02 s.
items.explanation: Δp_B = 5.3 × (0.23 − 0) = 1.219 kg·m·s⁻¹. F = Δp/Δt = 1.219/0.02 ≈ 60.95 N in direction of motion.

items.question: A spring between two trolleys releases trolley B (2.6 kg) at 0.492 m·s⁻¹. The spring exerts an average force of 4.2 N on B. Calculate the contact time of the spring with trolley B.

A bat exerts a force of 200 N for 0.05 s on a stationary ball. With a different bat the SAME change in momentum is achieved but the contact time is 0.20 s. What average force does the second bat exert?
items.explanation: Same Δp ⇒ F₁Δt₁ = F₂Δt₂. (200)(0.05) = F₂(0.20) ⇒ F₂ = 10/0.20 = 50 N. Quadrupling contact time quarters the average force.

items.question: An 800 kg car travelling west at 15 m·s⁻¹ collides with a 1200 kg car going east and the 800 kg car rebounds east at 7.5 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the impulse on the 800 kg car (east positive).
State the direction of the average force the bat exerts on the cricket ball (given the ball was initially moving toward the bat and rebounds in the opposite direction).
items.expectedAnswer: Opposite to the ball's initial velocity (the direction it moves after being hit).
items.explanation: The impulse (force × time) must reverse the ball's motion, so the force is in the new direction of motion.
options: Opposite to the ball's initial velocity (the direction it moves after being hit).
The same direction as the ball's initial velocity (toward the bat).

items.question: Define IMPULSE.
items.expectedAnswer: The product of the average force and the time it acts (J = FΔt); equals the change in momentum.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'F × Δt' + 'equals Δp / vector'.
options: The product of force and displacement.
The product of the average force and the time it acts (J = FΔt); equals the change in momentum.
The rate of change of momentum.

items.question: A 0.4 kg ball strikes a wall at 8 m·s⁻¹ and rebounds at 6 m·s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. Calculate the change in momentum.
items.explanation: Take initial direction positive. Δp = 0.4 × (−6 − 8) = 0.4 × (−14) = −5.6 kg·m·s⁻¹.

items.question: Continuing: contact with the wall lasts 0.01 s. Calculate the average force the wall exerts on the ball.
items.explanation: F = |Δp|/Δt = 5.6/0.01 = 560 N, in the direction the ball rebounds.

items.question: A car has airbags to reduce injury during a crash. Explain in terms of impulse why airbags help.
items.expectedAnswer: Δp is fixed; airbags increase the contact time Δt, so the average force F = Δp/Δt is smaller.
items.explanation: Same Δp, longer contact time ⇒ smaller force. The classic safety-by-impulse argument.
options: Airbags reduce the driver's change in momentum to nearly zero.
Airbags increase the force over a shorter time to stop the driver faster.
Δp is fixed; airbags increase the contact time Δt, so the average force F = Δp/Δt is smaller.

items.question: A 0.2 kg ball is at rest. A 5 N force is applied for 0.3 s. What is the final speed of the ball (no other forces)?
items.explanation: Impulse = FΔt = 5 × 0.3 = 1.5 N·s. Δp = m × v_f (since u = 0) ⇒ v_f = 1.5/0.2 = 7.5 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A force-time graph for a force on a 0.5 kg object shows a triangular pulse: force rises linearly from 0 to 80 N at t = 0.02 s, then decreases linearly back to 0 at t = 0.04 s. Calculate the change in momentum of the object.
items.explanation: Δp = area under F-t graph = area of triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 0.04 × 80 = 1.6 N·s = 1.6 kg·m·s⁻¹.

items.question: A 1500 kg car accelerates from 10 m·s⁻¹ to 25 m·s⁻¹ in 6 s. Calculate the impulse on the car.
items.explanation: Impulse = Δp = m(v − u) = 1500(25 − 10) = 1500 × 15 = 22 500 N·s in the direction of motion.

items.question: Following an internal explosion, part A of a rocket exerts a forward force F_AB on part B during a time interval. By Newton's Third Law, part B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. If F_AB is plotted as a positive rectangular pulse, sketch (in words) the force that B exerts on A as a function of time, and state the direction convention.
items.expectedAnswer: A pulse of equal magnitude but opposite direction (negative), over the same time interval.
items.explanation: Newton's Third Law in graphical form: equal magnitude, opposite sign, identical time interval.
options: A pulse of equal magnitude but opposite direction (negative), over the same time interval.
A pulse of equal magnitude in the same direction, over the same interval.
A larger pulse, because B is pushed harder than A.

items.question: An object has initial momentum p₁ rightward and final momentum p₂ rightward (with p₂ > p₁). The change in momentum Δp = p₂ − p₁ is therefore rightward (positive). On a graph showing momentum versus time, which feature represents this change?
items.expectedAnswer: The momentum–time curve rises from p₁ to p₂ (a positive, upward change).
items.explanation: Momentum increases ⇒ positive impulse ⇒ Δp positive. The vertical jump on p-t = impulse.
options: The curve falls from p₁ to p₂.
The momentum–time curve rises from p₁ to p₂ (a positive, upward change).
A horizontal line, since momentum is conserved.

items.question: A 0.06 kg tennis ball travelling at 25 m·s⁻¹ is caught and brought to rest in 0.3 s. Calculate the average force on the ball during the catch.
items.explanation: Δp = 0.06 × (0 − 25) = −1.5 kg·m·s⁻¹. F = Δp/Δt = −1.5/0.3 = −5 N (i.e. 5 N opposing the ball's motion).

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_IMPULSE_DEF: Definition of impulse missing F·Δt or Δp
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_FT_AREA_MEANING: Doesn't recognise area under F-t graph = impulse
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_IMPULSE_CONTACT_TIME: Misjudges how contact time affects average force

L5.T1.A1.skill_title: Explain and apply the Doppler equation for sound
L5.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 14 lifted, 6 fresh. Doppler effect for sound: definition, qualitative direction-of-shift, and Doppler-equation calculations for moving source or moving observer (or both). Speed of sound problems and wavelength.

items.question: Define the DOPPLER EFFECT.
items.expectedAnswer: The apparent change in the observed frequency (or pitch) of a wave as perceived by an observer, due to the relative motion between the source of the wave and the observer.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'apparent change in frequency' + 'relative motion between source and observer'. The actual source frequency does not change — only the observed value.

items.question: A source of sound moves TOWARDS a stationary observer. The frequency heard by the observer compared to the emitted frequency is:
items.expectedAnswer: Higher
items.explanation: Source approaching ⇒ wavefronts compressed ⇒ observed wavelength shorter ⇒ observed frequency higher.

items.question: An ambulance moves AWAY from a stationary person. The person hears the siren at a frequency that is:
items.expectedAnswer: Lower than emitted
items.explanation: Source receding ⇒ wavefronts stretched ⇒ longer wavelength ⇒ lower frequency.

items.question: A stationary source emits sound at 880 Hz. An observer in a car moves at 10 m·s⁻¹ TOWARDS the source. Calculate the frequency detected by the observer. (Speed of sound = 340 m·s⁻¹.)
items.explanation: Moving observer, stationary source: f_L = f_s × (v + v_L)/v = 880 × (340 + 10)/340 = 880 × 350/340 ≈ 905.9 Hz.

items.question: An ambulance siren emits 1200 Hz. The ambulance approaches a stationary observer at 30 m·s⁻¹. Speed of sound = 340 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard by the observer.
items.explanation: Moving source towards stationary observer: f_L = f_s × v/(v − v_s) = 1200 × 340/(340 − 30) = 1200 × 340/310 ≈ 1316 Hz.

items.question: Continuing: the ambulance passes the observer and moves away at the SAME 30 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the new observed frequency. (f_s = 1200 Hz, v = 340 m·s⁻¹.)
items.explanation: Source receding from stationary observer: f_L = f_s × v/(v + v_s) = 1200 × 340/(340 + 30) = 1200 × 340/370 ≈ 1102.7 Hz.

items.question: A train horn emits 850 Hz. The train moves at 25 m·s⁻¹ towards a station (stationary observer). Speed of sound = 340 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the observed frequency.
Continuing: train passes and moves away at 25 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the observed frequency.
A police car emits a siren of frequency f_s. A stationary recorder measures 615 Hz as the car approaches at 26 m·s⁻¹ and 526 Hz as it recedes at 26 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of sound in air.
Using v ≈ 333 m·s⁻¹ and the 615 Hz approaching reading from a 26 m·s⁻¹ police car, calculate the source frequency f_s and the wavelength of the siren.
A bat emits ultrasound of 50 000 Hz and receives the echo from a stationary cliff at 52 000 Hz. Speed of sound = 340 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the bat's speed.
items.explanation: Echo formula (double Doppler — bat is moving observer of a moving 'source' at the cliff that re-radiates the frequency the cliff detected): f_L = f_0(v + v_B)/(v − v_B). 52 000(340 − v_B) = 50 000(340 + v_B) ⇒ 1.04(340 − v_B) = 340 + v_B ⇒ 353.6 − 1.04 v_B = 340 + v_B ⇒ 13.6 = 2.04 v_B ⇒ v_B ≈ 6.67 m·s⁻¹.

items.question: Name ONE application of the Doppler effect in MEDICINE.
items.expectedAnswer: Examples: Doppler ultrasound to measure blood flow velocity; echocardiography (heart imaging); foetal heartbeat monitoring; detecting blocked arteries.
items.explanation: Any reasonable medical Doppler application earns the marks.

items.question: Give ONE application of the Doppler effect used by traffic authorities.
items.expectedAnswer: Speed traps / radar guns. Police use Doppler radar to measure the speed of moving vehicles by comparing the emitted radar frequency with the reflected (Doppler-shifted) frequency.
items.explanation: Standard application: traffic-enforcement speed radar.

items.question: A learner says: 'The Doppler shift occurs because the speed of sound changes.' Is this correct? Briefly explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. The speed of sound in a given medium is constant. The Doppler shift is caused by the relative motion of source and observer, which changes the WAVELENGTH (and hence the observed frequency) of the wavefronts received, NOT the wave speed.
items.explanation: Common misconception. v is fixed by the medium; λ changes due to relative motion ⇒ f_observed changes.

items.question: An observer is stationary. A source moves towards the observer at constant speed. Compared with when the source is stationary, the observed frequency is:
items.expectedAnswer: Higher and constant
items.explanation: While approaching at constant speed, the observed frequency is constantly higher than the source frequency. It stays HIGH (not gradually increasing or decreasing) until the source passes the observer.

items.question: A car moves at 20 m·s⁻¹ towards a stationary observer. The car horn emits 500 Hz. Speed of sound = 340 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the observed frequency.
A stationary siren emits 1000 Hz. A jogger runs AWAY from the siren at 5 m·s⁻¹. Speed of sound = 340 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency the jogger hears.
items.explanation: Moving observer receding: f_L = f_s × (v − v_L)/v = 1000 × 335/340 ≈ 985.3 Hz.

items.question: Two stationary observers stand on opposite sides of a road. A car drives past, sounding its horn. Which observer perceives the higher frequency, the one the car is moving TOWARDS, or the one the car is moving AWAY from?
items.expectedAnswer: Towards-observer perceives the higher frequency
items.explanation: Approaching observer: shorter wavelength ⇒ higher frequency. Receding observer: longer wavelength ⇒ lower frequency.

items.question: A 600 Hz source moves at 17 m·s⁻¹ towards a stationary observer (speed of sound 340 m·s⁻¹). Calculate the observed wavelength of the sound in front of the source.
items.explanation: Observed frequency: f_L = 600 × 340/(340 − 17) = 600 × 340/323 ≈ 631.6 Hz. Wavelength = v/f_L = 340/631.6 ≈ 0.538 m. Equivalently, λ_observed = (v − v_s)/f_s = 323/600 = 0.538 m.

items.question: A learner says: 'The actual frequency emitted by the siren changes when the ambulance approaches.' Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. The siren itself still emits the same frequency in its own frame. The Doppler effect changes the OBSERVED (perceived) frequency for an outside listener because the wavefronts arrive more often when the source approaches. The driver of the ambulance hears the normal siren frequency at all times.
items.explanation: The source frequency is fixed. The observed frequency depends on relative motion. Standard misconception.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_DOPPLER_DEF_ACTUAL_FREQ_CHANGE: Believes the source's actual emitted frequency changes

L5.T1.A2.skill_title: Apply the Doppler effect to astronomy (red shift and blue shift)
L5.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 6 lifted, 14 fresh. Astronomical Doppler: red shift (recession, longer wavelength) and blue shift (approach, shorter wavelength). Connection to expansion of the universe.

items.question: A star is moving AWAY from Earth. How does its light appear compared to if it were stationary?
items.expectedAnswer: Lower frequency (red shift)
items.explanation: Star moving away ⇒ wavelength stretched ⇒ shifts toward the RED end of the spectrum (longer wavelength, lower frequency).

items.question: A star is moving TOWARDS Earth. How does this star's light appear when observed from Earth?
items.expectedAnswer: Blue-shifted (higher frequency)
items.explanation: Star approaching ⇒ wavelength shortens ⇒ shifts toward the BLUE end of the spectrum (shorter wavelength, higher frequency).

items.question: A star appears BLUE-SHIFTED when observed from Earth. Which statement correctly describes its frequency (as observed) and its motion relative to Earth?
options: Observed frequency higher than source; star moving towards Earth
Observed frequency lower than source; star moving away from Earth
Observed frequency higher than source; star moving away from Earth
Observed frequency lower than source; star moving towards Earth
items.expectedAnswer: Observed frequency higher than source; star moving towards Earth
items.explanation: Blue shift = shorter wavelength = higher observed frequency = source approaching.

items.question: Stars A and B are both moving AWAY from Earth. The spectral lines of star B are MORE red-shifted than those of star A. Which conclusion is CORRECT?
options: Star B is closer to Earth than star A
Star A is moving faster than star B
Star B is moving faster (recession speed) than star A
Both stars are moving at the same speed
items.expectedAnswer: Star B is moving faster (recession speed) than star A
items.explanation: Greater red shift ⇒ larger fractional wavelength change ⇒ greater relative recession speed. Distance is not directly given by single-shot Doppler; it's the SPEED that determines the shift magnitude.

items.question: A star is moving AWAY from Earth. How does the frequency of its light observed on Earth compare to the source frequency? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: The observed frequency is LOWER than the source frequency (red shift). When the source moves away, successive wavefronts are emitted from further and further away, so they arrive at the observer with a longer interval — longer wavelength and lower observed frequency.
items.explanation: Standard recession explanation. Wavelength stretches, frequency drops.

items.question: An ambulance siren first sounds at a LOWER frequency than normal, then a HIGHER frequency. What does this indicate about the ambulance's motion?
items.expectedAnswer: Moving away, then approaching
items.explanation: Lower frequency ⇒ moving away (red shift). Higher frequency ⇒ moving towards (blue shift). So first away, then towards. (Acoustic analogue of red/blue shift.)

items.question: Most distant galaxies show a RED shift when observed from Earth. What does this tell us about the universe?
items.expectedAnswer: Most distant galaxies are moving AWAY from us, which means the universe is EXPANDING. (This is Hubble's observation: galaxies recede with speeds roughly proportional to their distance — the basis of the expanding-universe model.)
items.explanation: Red shift everywhere ⇒ galaxies receding ⇒ universe expanding. Foundational evidence for Big Bang cosmology.

items.question: Define RED SHIFT in the context of light from a star.
items.expectedAnswer: Red shift is the increase in observed wavelength (decrease in observed frequency) of light from a source that is moving AWAY from the observer. The light appears shifted toward the red end of the visible spectrum.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'longer wavelength / lower frequency' + 'source moving away'.

items.question: Define BLUE SHIFT in the context of light from a star.
items.expectedAnswer: Blue shift is the decrease in observed wavelength (increase in observed frequency) of light from a source that is moving TOWARDS the observer. The light appears shifted toward the blue end of the visible spectrum.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'shorter wavelength / higher frequency' + 'source approaching'.

items.question: Which of the following statements about red/blue shifts is FALSE?
options: Blue shift means the source is approaching
Red shift means the wavelength is longer than emitted
Greater shift magnitude ⇒ greater relative speed
A red shift means the star's actual emission frequency has decreased
items.expectedAnswer: A red shift means the star's actual emission frequency has decreased
items.explanation: The star's actual emission frequency does NOT change. Only the OBSERVED frequency on Earth differs because of relative motion (Doppler effect).

items.question: The light from a hydrogen line normally at 656 nm (red) is observed at 700 nm from a distant galaxy. What does this indicate?
options: Galaxy moving away from Earth, red-shifted
No motion; the hydrogen has different composition
items.expectedAnswer: Galaxy moving away from Earth, red-shifted
items.explanation: Observed wavelength (700) > source wavelength (656) ⇒ stretched ⇒ red shift ⇒ recession.

items.question: A hydrogen line is normally at 486 nm. A galaxy's light shows this line at 490 nm. Using Δλ/λ ≈ v/c (for v << c), estimate the recession speed of the galaxy. (c = 3 × 10⁸ m·s⁻¹.)
items.explanation: Δλ = 4 nm. Δλ/λ = 4/486 ≈ 0.00823. v ≈ 0.00823 × 3 × 10⁸ ≈ 2.47 × 10⁶ m·s⁻¹. (Note: the CAPS Doppler formula is for sound; this astronomical version is informational.)

items.question: If a distant galaxy is observed to be BLUE-shifted, what does this tell us about its motion?
options: It is moving away from Earth
items.expectedAnswer: It is moving towards Earth
items.explanation: Blue shift = shorter wavelength = approaching. (Andromeda Galaxy is the most famous nearby example.)

items.question: The Andromeda Galaxy shows a BLUE shift. What does this imply about Andromeda's motion relative to Earth?
items.expectedAnswer: Andromeda is moving TOWARDS the Milky Way (and Earth). Blue shift indicates approach, so the observed wavelength is shorter than emitted. Note that despite the overall expansion of the universe, nearby galaxies can still approach due to their local gravitational attraction.
items.explanation: Blue shift = approaching. Local gravitational pull can override cosmic expansion at short distances.

items.question: What property of a spectral line allows astronomers to detect a Doppler shift?
items.expectedAnswer: Its known rest wavelength (atomic origin)
items.explanation: Each element emits/absorbs at well-known rest wavelengths (e.g. hydrogen Balmer lines). Comparing observed wavelength to the known rest wavelength reveals the Doppler shift.

items.question: A distant quasar's hydrogen line is observed at TWICE its rest wavelength. Has it been red-shifted or blue-shifted, and what does that imply?
items.expectedAnswer: Red-shifted (observed wavelength longer than rest). It is moving away from Earth at a substantial fraction of the speed of light — a strong red shift indicates very large recession speed and great distance (consistent with the expanding universe).
items.explanation: λ_observed > λ_rest ⇒ red shift. Large shift ⇒ large recession speed.

items.question: A learner asks: 'If we see a star's light shifted to a longer wavelength, did the star really emit different light?' Briefly explain.
items.expectedAnswer: No, the star emitted the SAME (rest-frame) light. The shift is in the OBSERVED wavelength due to the star's motion relative to Earth. From the star's own frame, its emission spectrum is unchanged.
items.explanation: Source frequency in the star's frame is constant. Doppler shift is a frame-dependent observation.

items.question: If a star is BOTH bright AND red-shifted, what does each piece of information tell us?
items.expectedAnswer: Brightness alone does not tell us its speed — only its apparent intensity. The red shift tells us the star is moving AWAY from us. Combining brightness with known stellar properties can suggest distance, but the red-shift specifically indicates recession.
items.explanation: Brightness ≠ shift. Red shift = motion (away).

items.question: Which of the following is the MOST important consequence of the observation that most galaxies are red-shifted?
options: Earth is at the centre of the universe
items.expectedAnswer: The universe is expanding
items.explanation: Universal red shift ⇒ galaxies receding ⇒ expanding universe (the basic evidence for Big Bang cosmology).

items.question: Compare red shift and blue shift in one sentence each.
items.expectedAnswer: Red shift: observed wavelength LONGER than rest wavelength, indicating the source is moving AWAY. Blue shift: observed wavelength SHORTER than rest wavelength, indicating the source is moving TOWARDS the observer.
items.explanation: Two clean one-liners describing each shift and its direction implication.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RED_BLUE_REVERSE: Swaps the direction of red and blue shifts
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SHIFT_DIRECTION: Wrong direction of approach/recession given the shift
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_REDSHIFT_DISTANCE_VS_SPEED: Equates shift magnitude with distance instead of speed
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_EXPANDING_UNIVERSE: Doesn't connect universal red shift to expansion
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RED_DEFINITION: Red shift definition incomplete or wrong
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BLUE_DEFINITION: Blue shift definition incomplete or wrong
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_DOPPLER_DEF_ACTUAL_FREQ_CHANGE: Believes the star's actual emission frequency changes
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_REDSHIFT_DETECTION: Doesn't link known atomic rest wavelengths to shift detection

L6.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply Coulomb's Law to calculate force between point charges
L6.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 11 lifted, 9 fresh. Coulomb's Law definition + force between two point charges; signs; inverse-square law; sharing charge through contact.

items.question: State COULOMB'S LAW in words.
items.expectedAnswer: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force acts along the line joining the two charges.
items.explanation: Three marks: 'product of charges' + 'inversely proportional to r²' + 'along line joining charges'. F = kQ₁Q₂/r².

items.question: Two point charges Q and 2Q are separated by distance r. The electrostatic force between them is F. If the distance is DOUBLED, the new force is:
items.explanation: F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r ⇒ 1/r² × ¼ ⇒ F becomes F/4.

items.question: Sphere X has charge +2q and sphere Y has charge −6q. They are brought into contact and then separated. The original force between them was F. What is the new force after contact?
items.explanation: Originally |F| ∝ |2q × 6q| = 12q². After contact (identical spheres): total charge −4q shared equally ⇒ −2q each. |F'| ∝ |2q × 2q| = 4q². Ratio = 4/12 = 1/3 (magnitude). So new force = F/3 (now repulsive, both negative).

items.question: Sphere R has charge +5 × 10⁻⁹ C and sphere S has charge −6 × 10⁻⁹ C. The electrostatic force between them is 1.2 × 10⁻³ N (attractive). Calculate the distance r between R and S. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Charges X (−7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C) and Y (+7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C) are placed 0.03 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Two small charged spheres A (+4 μC) and B (−6 μC) are placed 0.03 m apart in air. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between Q₁ = +4 × 10⁻⁶ C and Q₂ = −6 × 10⁻⁶ C placed 0.3 m apart. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Q₁ = +5 × 10⁻⁶ C and Q₂ = +5 × 10⁻⁶ C are placed 0.4 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive. (k = 9 × 10⁹.)
items.explanation: Same-sign charges repel. F ≈ 1.41 N along the line joining the charges, directed outward from each.

items.question: Two opposite charges (one positive, one negative) are released from rest and move towards each other under their mutual attraction. Which statement best describes the ACCELERATION of each charge as they approach?
items.expectedAnswer: Acceleration increases as r decreases
items.explanation: F = kq₁q₂/r². As they approach, r decreases ⇒ F increases ⇒ a = F/m increases. (Both charges accelerate more rapidly the closer they get.)

items.question: Two charges 5 nC and −2 nC are 0.10 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)

Two identical metal spheres carry equal positive charges of +6 μC each. The force between them is 4 N. They are then touched together (so they share charge equally) and returned to the same positions. What is the new force between them?
items.explanation: Touching identical spheres shares total charge equally — each still ends up with +6 μC (because they already had equal charges). So the force is unchanged: 4 N.

items.question: Two metal spheres carry charges of +8 μC and +2 μC and the force between them is F. They are briefly touched together and returned to their positions. What is the new force in terms of F?
items.explanation: Original: F ∝ 8 × 2 = 16. After contact: each sphere has (8+2)/2 = +5 μC. New ∝ 5 × 5 = 25. Ratio = 25/16. F' = (25/16)F.

items.question: A learner says: 'Coulomb's force can have a negative magnitude.' Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: No. Force MAGNITUDE is always positive. The negative sign in F = kQ₁Q₂/r² when one charge is negative just tells us the force is ATTRACTIVE (not 'pointing in the negative direction'). When reporting magnitudes, take the absolute value of the charges in the formula.
items.explanation: The sign of Coulomb's force tells you attraction (negative product) or repulsion (positive product), not direction. Magnitude is a positive scalar.

items.question: Calculate how many electrons must be removed from a neutral sphere to give it a charge of +1.6 nC. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
items.explanation: n = Q/e = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 10¹⁰ = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ electrons removed.

items.question: Two point charges experience a force of 10 N when 1 m apart. What is the force when they are moved to 0.5 m apart?
items.explanation: F ∝ 1/r². Halving r ⇒ F × 4. New F = 40 N.

items.question: Two point charges experience a force of 24 N. If one of the charges is TRIPLED while the distance is kept the same, what is the new force?
items.explanation: F ∝ Q₁ × Q₂. Tripling one charge triples F. New F = 72 N.

items.question: An electron and a proton are separated by 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
What is the SI unit of charge?
items.expectedAnswer: Coulomb (C)
items.explanation: 1 C = charge transported by 1 A for 1 s.

items.question: Two point charges Q and Q each repel one another with a force of 100 N. If both charges are HALVED and the distance between them is HALVED, what is the new force?
items.explanation: F ∝ Q₁Q₂/r². Halve each Q ⇒ multiply by ¼. Halve r ⇒ multiply by 4. Net change: ¼ × 4 = 1. Force unchanged at 100 N.

items.question: Which TWO requirements does Coulomb's Law strictly assume about the charged objects?
items.expectedAnswer: (1) The charges must be POINT CHARGES (or behave as such — small spheres at large separations approximate this). (2) The charges must be at REST relative to each other (or moving slowly enough that magnetic effects are negligible). Also: the medium is usually assumed to be vacuum/air.
items.explanation: Point charges + at rest + uniform medium. For spheres, the centre-to-centre distance is used.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_INVERSE_SQUARE_LAW: Misapplies inverse-square scaling (e.g. halves F when r doubles)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_CHARGE_SHARING: Doesn't equally share charge between identical spheres in contact

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_REARRANGE: Algebra mistake when solving F = kQ₁Q₂/r² for r or Q
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_R_SQUARED: Forgets to square r in denominator
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_RATIO: Wrong scaling when changing Q and r simultaneously
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_CHARGE_QUANTIZED: Forgets Q = n·e for counting electrons
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_ASSUMPTIONS: Can't state the point-charge / at-rest assumptions

L6.T1.A2.skill_title: Calculate electric field at a point (single and net)
L6.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 9 lifted, 11 fresh. Electric field E = kQ/r² from a single point charge; vector addition of fields from multiple charges; field-line patterns; E-vs-Q and E-vs-1/r² graphical analysis.

items.question: The magnitude of the electric field at a distance r from a point charge Q is given by:
items.expectedAnswer: kQ/r²
items.explanation: E = F/q (for a test charge q) = kQ/r². Inverse-square law, just like Coulomb's force.

items.question: Which graph CORRECTLY shows the relationship between the electric field E and the magnitude of charge Q at a FIXED distance?
items.expectedAnswer: Straight line through origin (E ∝ Q)
items.explanation: E = kQ/r². At fixed r, E ∝ Q. Linear graph through the origin with positive gradient.

items.question: Calculate the electric field at point X, which is 0.025 m from a +4 nC point charge. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Calculate the electric field at the midpoint between Q₁ = +5 × 10⁻⁶ C and Q₂ = +5 × 10⁻⁶ C placed 0.4 m apart, due to Q₁ ONLY. (Midpoint is 0.2 m from each.)
items.explanation: E_Q1 = kQ/r² = (9×10⁹)(5×10⁻⁶)/(0.2²) = 45 000/0.04 = 1.125 × 10⁶ N·C⁻¹, directed away from Q₁ (towards Q₂).

items.question: Describe the electric field pattern around an ISOLATED POSITIVELY charged sphere. (You may describe instead of drawing.)
items.expectedAnswer: Field lines radiate OUTWARD from the centre of the positive sphere in all directions (radially). Lines are straight, evenly spaced near the sphere, and decrease in density (further apart) as r increases — reflecting that the field weakens with distance.
items.explanation: Three marks: outward direction + radial pattern + density decreases with r.

items.question: Describe (in words) the electric field pattern around a +4 nC point charge.
items.expectedAnswer: Radially outward from the +4 nC charge in all directions. At least 8 evenly spaced straight arrows pointing away. Lines are denser near the charge and farther apart with distance.
items.explanation: Positive ⇒ outward arrows. Spacing reflects field magnitude.

items.question: Two charged spheres S and T are placed near each other. The electric field lines run from S to T (originating at S, terminating at T). What is the SIGN of each sphere?
items.expectedAnswer: S positive, T negative
items.explanation: Field lines start on positive charges (S) and end on negative charges (T). Conventional rule: out of +, into −.

items.question: A graph of electric field E versus 1/r² is plotted for a charged sphere. What does the SHAPE of this graph indicate about the relationship between E and 1/r²?
items.expectedAnswer: If the graph is a straight line through the origin, E is directly proportional to 1/r² — i.e. E = kQ × (1/r²). The gradient of the line equals kQ.
items.explanation: Linear E vs 1/r² ⇒ confirms inverse-square dependence of E on r. Gradient gives kQ.

items.question: The gradient of an E vs 1/r² graph for charge A is 680 N·m²·C⁻¹. Calculate the charge on sphere A. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
items.explanation: Gradient = kQ ⇒ Q = gradient/k = 680/(9×10⁹) ≈ 7.56 × 10⁻⁸ C.

items.question: Two charges, Q₁ = +6 nC and Q₂ = −6 nC, are placed 0.20 m apart on a horizontal line. Calculate the magnitude of the NET electric field at the midpoint between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹.)
items.explanation: At the midpoint (0.10 m from each): E_Q1 = (9×10⁹)(6×10⁻⁹)/(0.1²) = 5400 N·C⁻¹ pointing away from Q₁ (towards Q₂). E_Q2 = 5400 N·C⁻¹ pointing towards Q₂ (so same direction). Same direction ⇒ add: E_net = 10 800 N·C⁻¹.

items.question: Two equal POSITIVE charges Q₁ = +5 μC and Q₂ = +5 μC are placed 0.40 m apart. Calculate the NET electric field at the midpoint between them.
items.explanation: At the midpoint, E_Q1 and E_Q2 have equal magnitudes but OPPOSITE directions (each points away from its own +). They cancel ⇒ net E = 0.

items.question: Define ELECTRIC FIELD at a point.
items.expectedAnswer: The electric field at a point is the electrostatic force per unit positive test charge experienced at that point: E = F/q. It is a vector quantity with direction the same as the force on a positive test charge. SI unit: newton per coulomb (N·C⁻¹) or volt per metre (V·m⁻¹).
items.explanation: Two marks: 'force per unit positive test charge' + 'vector / N·C⁻¹'.

items.question: An electric field of 200 N·C⁻¹ acts on a point charge of −5 nC at a point. Calculate the magnitude of the force on the charge.
items.explanation: F = |E·q| = 200 × 5 × 10⁻⁹ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ N. Direction is opposite to E (because charge is negative).

items.question: Two charges of +3 μC and +3 μC are placed at the corners of a square (diagonal opposite). At the centre of the square, what is the magnitude of the net electric field?
options: Equal to the field from one charge alone
Twice the field from one charge alone
items.expectedAnswer: Zero
items.explanation: Equal positive charges at equal distances on opposite sides ⇒ fields at the centre are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction ⇒ cancel ⇒ net zero.

items.question: A learner draws field lines for a NEGATIVE point charge with arrows pointing OUTWARD. What's wrong?
items.expectedAnswer: Field lines around a negative charge must point INWARD (towards the charge). By convention, lines start on positive charges and END on negative charges. A negative charge alone has field lines coming inward from infinity.
items.explanation: Convention: + outward, − inward. Critical for getting field patterns right.

items.question: Charges X (−7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C) at origin, Y (+7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C) at 0.03 m to the right, and Z (positive, magnitude unknown) at 0.01 m to the LEFT of X. The resultant electric field at point X is 4.91 × 10⁵ N·C⁻¹ directed to the RIGHT. Calculate the magnitude of charge Z.
items.explanation: Find E from Y at X: E_Y = (9×10⁹)(7.2×10⁻⁹)/(0.03²) ≈ 72 000 N·C⁻¹ toward Y (right). Net E at X = 4.91×10⁵ N·C⁻¹ right. So E from Z = 4.91×10⁵ − 7.2×10⁴ = 4.19×10⁵ N·C⁻¹ (right). Z is positive and 0.01 m left of X, so its field at X also points right (away from +Z). E_Z = kQ_Z/r² ⇒ Q_Z = E_Z × r²/k = 4.19×10⁵ × (0.01²)/(9×10⁹) ≈ 4.66 × 10⁻⁹ C.

items.question: Which TWO conditions are NOT consistent with electric field lines?
options: Lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges
Lines can split or join at points
Lines indicate the direction of force on a positive test charge
items.expectedAnswer: Lines can split or join at points
items.explanation: Field lines never cross (E has a unique direction at each point). They don't split or join. They start on + and end on −, and show the direction of force on a positive test charge.

items.question: A 2 μC charge is at the origin. Calculate the electric field at a point P, 0.30 m to the right of the charge. State magnitude AND direction. (k = 9 × 10⁹.)
items.expectedAnswer: E = kQ/r² = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁶)/(0.3²) = 18 000/0.09 = 2 × 10⁵ N·C⁻¹. Direction: AWAY from the +2 μC charge — i.e. to the RIGHT at point P.
items.explanation: Magnitude from kQ/r². Direction: away from positive charge.

items.question: On an E vs 1/r² graph plotted for two charged spheres, sphere B's gradient is GREATER than sphere A's. Compare the charges on B and A and explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Sphere B has a GREATER charge than sphere A. The gradient of E vs 1/r² is kQ, so a steeper gradient implies a larger Q.
items.explanation: Gradient = kQ. Same k for both. Bigger gradient ⇒ bigger Q.

items.question: Three charges sit on a horizontal line: Q₁ = +4 μC at x = 0, Q₂ = −2 μC at x = 0.5 m. Calculate the magnitude of the net electric field at x = 1.0 m (i.e. 1.0 m right of Q₁, 0.5 m right of Q₂). (k = 9 × 10⁹.)
items.explanation: E_Q1 at (1,0) = (9×10⁹)(4×10⁻⁶)/(1.0²) = 36 000 N·C⁻¹ to the right (away from +). E_Q2 at (1,0) = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁶)/(0.5²) = 72 000 N·C⁻¹ to the LEFT (towards −Q₂). E_net = 72 000 − 36 000 = 36 000 N·C⁻¹ to the LEFT. (Magnitude 36 000 N·C⁻¹.)

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_E_FIELD_FORMULA: Wrong formula for E from a point charge
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_E_VS_Q_GRAPH: Misreads E-vs-Q relation at fixed r
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_E_FIELD_R_SQUARED: Forgets to square r in E = kQ/r²
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_E_FIELD_DIRECTION: Wrong direction for E (towards + or away from −)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_FIELD_LINE_DENSITY: Doesn't link field line density to field strength
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_FIELD_LINE_TERMINATE: Doesn't recognise lines start on + and end on −
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_E_FIELD_VECTOR_ADD: Adds field magnitudes when they point in opposite directions
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_E_FIELD_DEF: E definition missing 'per unit positive test charge'
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_FIELD_LINE_CROSSING: Believes field lines can cross or branch

L6.T1.A3.skill_title: Combine electric force with mechanics (FBDs including electric forces)
L6.T1.A3.notes: 20 items: 8 lifted, 12 fresh. Mechanics problems where electrostatic forces appear on the FBD — equilibrium of suspended/inclined charged objects, charged ball motion in a field, summing vector forces with electric contributions.

items.question: Q₁ = +5 μC and Q₂ = +5 μC are placed 0.4 m apart on a horizontal line. A third charge Q₃ = −2 μC is placed midway between them (0.2 m from each). Calculate the magnitude of the net electrostatic force on Q₃ and state its direction. (k = 9 × 10⁹.)
items.expectedAnswer: F from each +5 μC on Q₃: F₁ = (9×10⁹)(5×10⁻⁶)(2×10⁻⁶)/(0.2²) = 90×10⁻³/0.04 = 2.25 N (attractive, towards each + charge). The two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction along the line ⇒ they CANCEL. Net force = 0 N.
items.explanation: Symmetric configuration: two equal attractive forces in opposite directions cancel. Net force is zero (this is a classic equilibrium check).

items.question: Q₁ = +4 × 10⁻⁶ C at A, Q₂ = −6 × 10⁻⁶ C at B (0.3 m to the right of A). Test charge Q₃ = +1 × 10⁻⁶ C at C, which is 0.2 m to the right of B (i.e. 0.5 m from A). Calculate the net force on Q₃ and state its direction.
items.expectedAnswer: F₁ (Q₁ on Q₃): (9×10⁹)(4×10⁻⁶)(1×10⁻⁶)/(0.5²) = 0.144 N to the RIGHT (both +, repulsive). F₂ (Q₂ on Q₃): (9×10⁹)(6×10⁻⁶)(1×10⁻⁶)/(0.2²) = 1.35 N to the LEFT (Q₂ −, Q₃ +, attractive ⇒ towards Q₂, i.e. left). Net F = 1.35 − 0.144 = 1.206 N to the LEFT.
items.explanation: Compute each force separately with the correct direction, then sum as vectors along the line.

items.question: Two polystyrene balls A and B (each 0.012 kg) hang from the ceiling. A is neutral; B carries charge Q_B. The balls are 9° apart at the strings (each hanging at 9° from vertical when in equilibrium). Calculate the electrostatic force F_E on ball B. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: For ball B in equilibrium: T sin9° = F_E (horizontal) and T cos9° = mg (vertical). Dividing: tan9° = F_E/(mg) ⇒ F_E = mg tan9° = 0.012 × 9.8 × 0.1584 ≈ 0.0186 N.

items.question: Charge X (−7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C) lies between Y (+7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C, 0.03 m to the right of X) and Z (positive, 0.01 m to the LEFT of X). Draw or describe a vector diagram showing all electric forces acting on X.
items.expectedAnswer: Force by Y on X: Y is positive and X negative ⇒ ATTRACTIVE ⇒ force points from X TOWARDS Y, i.e. to the RIGHT. Force by Z on X: Z is positive and X negative ⇒ attractive ⇒ force points from X TOWARDS Z, i.e. to the LEFT. The two forces act in opposite directions along the same horizontal line.
items.explanation: Each force has a sign relative to the charge pair: opposite signs ⇒ attractive (towards the other charge).

items.question: Sphere S (mass 0.01 kg, charge −6 nC) sits on a 25° smooth incline and is held in equilibrium by a light string connecting it (along the incline) to sphere R (+5 nC) located further down the slope. Describe (or sketch) the free-body diagram for sphere S, including the electrostatic force.
items.expectedAnswer: Forces on S (all from a single dot): (1) Weight mg vertically DOWN; (2) Normal N perpendicular to the inclined surface (pointing away from surface); (3) Tension T along the string (toward R, i.e. down the slope or along the line joining S to R); (4) Electrostatic force F_RS along the line joining R and S — since R is positive and S is negative, F is ATTRACTIVE on S, pointing from S towards R.
items.explanation: Standard incline FBD with the electrostatic force added as a fourth vector along the S–R line.

items.question: Sphere S (mass 0.01 kg, charge −6 nC) sits on a 25° smooth incline, held in equilibrium by a string connecting it along the incline to sphere R (+5 nC) located further down the slope. Tension T in the string acts on S along the incline (toward R, i.e. downslope) and the electrostatic attraction F_RS also pulls S toward R (downslope). The normal force is perpendicular to the slope and weight is vertical. Set up the equilibrium equation along the slope and solve for T, given F_RS ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻³ N.
items.expectedAnswer: Along the slope (take up-slope positive): weight component down-slope = mg sin25° = 0.01 × 9.8 × sin25° ≈ 0.0414 N. Equilibrium: T + F_RS (both pulling S downslope toward R) − mg sin25° = 0 (only if T and F_RS are upslope — depends on geometry). For the geometry where R is downslope, F_RS pulls S toward R (downslope) AND T pulls S toward R (downslope), in which case: 0 = T + F_RS − mg sin25° (if there's another upslope force). In the original paper layout, with S held by string against gravity: T (up-slope) balances mg sin25° and F_RS (downslope). T = mg sin25° + F_RS ≈ 0.0414 + 0.0012 = 0.0426 N. (Marker note: answer depends on the precise diagram; check carefully.)
items.explanation: Set up Newton's First Law along the slope including the electrostatic attraction. T balances both mg sinθ and F_RS if they pull S downslope.

items.question: Two identical positive charges Q sit at points P and Q on a horizontal line. A NEGATIVE test charge q is placed exactly halfway between them. What is the net force on q?
options: Toward both (net force is the sum of the two)
items.expectedAnswer: Zero, by symmetry
items.explanation: At the midpoint, the two attractive forces from P and Q are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction along the horizontal line. They cancel ⇒ net force zero.

items.question: A 0.005 kg pith ball carries a charge of +20 nC. It hangs from a thread between the plates of a horizontal capacitor that creates a uniform horizontal electric field of 2 × 10⁵ N·C⁻¹. The thread makes an angle θ with the vertical. Calculate θ.
A small charged sphere (mass 0.002 kg, charge +5 μC) sits at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal electric field of 1000 N·C⁻¹ is applied. Calculate the sphere's acceleration.
items.explanation: Electric force = qE = 5×10⁻⁶ × 1000 = 0.005 N. a = F/m = 0.005/0.002 = 2.5 m·s⁻² in the direction of E (since q is positive).

items.question: A 0.001 kg ball with charge +3 nC is released from rest in a uniform downward electric field of 5 × 10⁵ N·C⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the ball's downward acceleration. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
items.explanation: F_E (down, positive charge in downward E) = qE = 3×10⁻⁹ × 5×10⁵ = 1.5×10⁻³ N. Weight = mg = 0.001 × 9.8 = 9.8×10⁻³ N (down). Net = 11.3×10⁻³ N. a = F/m = 11.3 m·s⁻² (downward).

items.question: A learner draws the FBD for a charged sphere hanging between two parallel plates (one + and one −, vertical orientation). They include weight downward and tension along the string but omit the electric force. What's missing?
items.expectedAnswer: The electrostatic force on the charged sphere due to the uniform field between the plates is missing. It should be drawn as a HORIZONTAL arrow on the dot, in the direction qE (positive charge ⇒ from + plate to − plate; negative charge ⇒ opposite). Without it, the FBD doesn't account for the equilibrium that causes the string to tilt.
items.explanation: Critical FBD principle: every force present must appear. Electric force is its own arrow alongside weight and tension.

items.question: Two identical charged spheres, mass 0.05 kg each, are 0.10 m apart on a frictionless horizontal surface. Each has charge +Q. The repulsive force gives each an acceleration of 0.2 m·s⁻². Calculate Q. (k = 9 × 10⁹.)

A pith ball (mass 0.001 kg) on a 0.5 m thread is deflected sideways by a uniform horizontal electric field. In equilibrium, the thread makes 15° with the vertical. Calculate the horizontal electric force on the ball. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
An electron (charge −e) is at rest in a uniform downward electric field. To keep it stationary (not free-fall), the field must produce an upward force on it. Which direction does the field point?
items.expectedAnswer: Downward
items.explanation: Force on a negative charge is OPPOSITE to E. For an upward force on the electron, E must point DOWNWARD. (qE is upward when q < 0 and E is downward.)

items.question: A 0.002 kg charged sphere (charge unknown) is suspended in equilibrium by a thread that makes 30° with the vertical inside a horizontal uniform electric field of 4 × 10⁴ N·C⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the charge on the sphere. (g = 9.8 m·s⁻².)
An oil droplet of mass m and charge −Q is HELD STATIONARY between horizontal parallel plates. The lower plate is positive. What is the magnitude of the electric field E between the plates?
items.expectedAnswer: For the droplet to be stationary, the upward electric force on the negative charge must balance gravity: qE = mg ⇒ E = mg/Q. The field between the plates points UPWARD (from + lower plate to − upper plate? no — from + to − is downward; the upward force on −Q from a downward E equals qE upward, which balances mg).
items.explanation: Classic Millikan-style equilibrium. E points from + to −. Force on negative charge is opposite to E. The condition is qE = mg.

items.question: Two charged balls hang from a common point by strings of equal length. Each has mass 0.001 kg and charge +Q. In equilibrium, each string makes 5° with the vertical and the balls are 0.06 m apart. Calculate Q. (k = 9 × 10⁹, g = 9.8.)
A charged particle accelerates due to an electric field alone. As the field strength doubles, what happens to the acceleration?
items.expectedAnswer: Doubles
items.explanation: F = qE; a = F/m = qE/m. E doubles ⇒ a doubles.

items.question: A horizontal uniform electric field of 5000 N·C⁻¹ acts on a 1 g ball with charge +4 μC. The ball sits on a frictionless horizontal surface. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the ball's acceleration.
items.expectedAnswer: F = qE = 4×10⁻⁶ × 5000 = 0.02 N (in the direction of E). a = F/m = 0.02/0.001 = 20 m·s⁻² in the same direction as E (because q > 0).
items.explanation: Force on positive charge is along E. a = qE/m.

items.question: On the FBD of a charged sphere sitting on a horizontal frictionless surface in a vertical electric field pointing UP, with the sphere positive, list the forces and their directions.
items.expectedAnswer: Three forces (all from a single dot): (1) Weight mg DOWN; (2) Normal force N UP from the surface; (3) Electrostatic force qE UP (positive charge in an upward field). Net force balance (vertical, no acceleration if sphere stays on surface): N + qE = mg. If qE > mg the sphere lifts off.
items.explanation: Three vertical forces; note that the electric force can be in either vertical direction depending on field/charge signs.

L7.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply Ohm's Law and calculate resistance in series and parallel circuits
L7.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 12 lifted, 8 fresh. Definitions of EMF/current/potential difference; Ohm's Law V=IR; series and parallel resistance combinations; circuit reduction.

items.question: State OHM'S LAW in words.
items.expectedAnswer: The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature (and other physical conditions) remain constant.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'I ∝ V' + 'at constant temperature'. The temperature condition is essential — without it, the law isn't strictly true for many conductors.

items.question: Define an OHMIC CONDUCTOR.
items.expectedAnswer: An ohmic conductor is one that obeys Ohm's Law — the ratio V/I (resistance) remains constant at constant temperature. A V-I graph for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'obeys Ohm's law / V/I = constant' + 'at constant temperature' (or linear V-I graph through origin).

items.question: In an electric circuit, a VOLTMETER should be connected:
options: In series with the component, with low resistance
In parallel with the component, with high resistance
items.expectedAnswer: In parallel with the component, with high resistance
items.explanation: A voltmeter measures p.d. ACROSS a component ⇒ parallel connection. High internal resistance prevents it from drawing significant current that would disturb the circuit.

items.question: R₂ = 6 Ω and R₃ = 3 Ω are connected in PARALLEL. Calculate the equivalent resistance of this parallel combination.
Continuing: R₁ = 4 Ω is connected in SERIES with the parallel combination (R₂ ∥ R₃ = 2 Ω from previous). Calculate the total external resistance.
items.explanation: Series: R_ext = R₁ + R_p = 4 + 2 = 6 Ω.

items.question: R₂ = 4 Ω and R₃ = 6 Ω in PARALLEL. Calculate the equivalent parallel resistance.
A battery (ε = 12 V, r = 0.5 Ω) drives a current of 1.85 A through R_ext = 6 Ω (R₁ = 4 Ω in series with R_p = 2 Ω). Calculate the p.d. across the parallel combination.
The parallel combination has p.d. 3.69 V across it. R₂ = 6 Ω is one branch. Calculate the current through R₂.
Ammeter A1 reads 1.5 A through a 3 Ω resistor. Calculate the power dissipated in the 3 Ω resistor.
R₁ is in SERIES with the parallel combination of R₂ and R₃ (all identical resistance R). The power dissipated in R₁ is P. What is the power dissipated in R₂?
items.explanation: R_parallel = R/2. Total R = 3R/2. I_total flows through R₁ and splits equally between R₂ and R₃. P_R1 = I²R. P_R2 = (I/2)²R = I²R/4 = P/4.

items.question: A battery is connected to a 4 Ω external resistor. When the main switch is closed, V_terminal across the 4 Ω resistor is 3.2 V. Calculate the current through it.
A circuit has 4 identical resistors with 4 ammeters (A1 in main line, A2/A3/A4 across three parallel branches). Which ammeter generally gives the LOWEST reading?
options: A3 or A4 (branches with higher resistance)
items.expectedAnswer: A3 or A4 (branches with higher resistance)
items.explanation: In a parallel network, less current flows through branches with higher resistance (I = V_p / R_branch). A1 in the main line carries the largest current.

items.question: Define POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE between two points in a circuit.
items.expectedAnswer: The energy transferred per unit positive charge passing between the two points. p.d. = energy/charge = W/Q. SI unit: volt (V = J/C).
items.explanation: Two marks: 'energy per unit charge' + 'between two points / volt'.

items.question: A 6 V battery is connected to three resistors in SERIES: 1 Ω, 2 Ω, and 3 Ω. Calculate the current in the circuit. (Ignore internal resistance.)
Two 6 Ω resistors are connected in PARALLEL. What is the equivalent resistance?
items.explanation: 1/R_p = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 ⇒ R_p = 3 Ω. Two equal resistors in parallel ⇒ half of each.

items.question: In a circuit, a 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. Calculate the current drawn from the battery (no internal resistance).
Which of the following statements about SERIES circuits is CORRECT?
options: Current is the same everywhere; voltages add
Voltage is the same everywhere; currents add
Both voltage and current are the same
items.expectedAnswer: Current is the same everywhere; voltages add
items.explanation: Series: single loop ⇒ same I throughout. Each resistor drops part of the EMF ⇒ V_total = V₁ + V₂ + ... Resistances add.

items.question: Which of the following statements about PARALLEL circuits is CORRECT?
options: Current is the same in all branches; voltages add
Voltage across each branch is the same; currents through branches add to give total
Both voltage and current are the same in all branches
Branches with higher R carry more current
items.expectedAnswer: Voltage across each branch is the same; currents through branches add to give total
items.explanation: Parallel: same V across each branch (they share endpoints). I_total = I₁ + I₂ + … 1/R_p adds. Higher-R branches carry LESS current.

items.question: A 10 V battery is connected to a 5 Ω resistor. Find the (a) current, (b) power dissipated in the resistor.
A learner says: 'Adding resistors in parallel always DECREASES the equivalent resistance.' Is this correct? Briefly explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Yes — correct. Adding a new branch in parallel always provides an additional path for current, increasing total conductance (1/R_p adds), so R_p decreases. The equivalent resistance of any parallel combination is LESS than the smallest individual resistor.
items.explanation: Adding parallel ⇒ R decreases. Adding series ⇒ R increases.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_PARALLEL_CURRENT_SHARING: Doesn't apportion current correctly between branches

L7.T1.A2.skill_title: Solve circuit problems with internal resistance
L7.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 13 lifted, 7 fresh. EMF = I(R + r); terminal voltage; reading EMF from an open switch; effect on terminal voltage when R is added or removed.

items.question: Define EMF of a battery in TWO ways: (a) in terms of energy, and (b) as measured directly in a circuit.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Energy definition: The EMF is the energy (work done) per unit charge supplied by the battery, or equivalently the total energy per coulomb when no charge is delivered. (b) Circuit definition: The EMF equals the terminal voltage when no current flows (open-circuit voltage), i.e. when the external switch is open.
items.explanation: (a) ε = W/Q (energy per charge); (b) ε = V_terminal at I = 0.

items.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY defines the EMF of a cell?
options: The potential difference across the terminals when current flows
The maximum energy (work done) per unit charge by the cell
The product of current and external resistance
The internal resistance times the current
items.expectedAnswer: The maximum energy (work done) per unit charge by the cell
items.explanation: EMF = max work per coulomb = total energy supplied per charge by the cell.

items.question: In a circuit, the terminal voltage of a battery equals its EMF when:
items.expectedAnswer: No current flows
items.explanation: V_terminal = ε − Ir. When I = 0 (open switch), V_terminal = ε.

items.question: A voltmeter across a battery reads 2.8 V when the external switch is OPEN and 2.63 V when the switch is closed (current 0.85 A flows). Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
items.explanation: Open: ε = 2.8 V. Closed: V_terminal = 2.63 V. V_lost = ε − V_terminal = 0.17 V. V_lost = Ir ⇒ r = 0.17/0.85 = 0.2 Ω.

items.question: Continuing: the voltmeter reads 2.8 V with the switch OPEN. What is the EMF of the battery?
items.explanation: Open switch ⇒ I = 0 ⇒ V_terminal = ε. So ε = 2.8 V (the open-circuit voltmeter reading).

items.question: A 4 Ω resistor draws 0.8 A from a battery with internal resistance r = 0.5 Ω, giving terminal voltage 3.2 V across the resistor. Calculate the EMF of the battery.
Explain why a battery HEATS UP during operation.
items.expectedAnswer: Current flows through the battery's internal resistance r. This dissipates power P = I²r as HEAT in the battery, raising its temperature.
items.explanation: Internal resistance ⇒ power lost as heat. The bigger I or r, the more heating.

items.question: A battery (ε = 12 V, r = 0.5 Ω) drives a circuit with external resistance 6 Ω. Calculate the current from the battery.
Continuing: with I = 1.85 A and r = 0.5 Ω, calculate the terminal voltage of the battery.
A battery (ε = 9 V, r = 1 Ω) drives a circuit with external resistance 5.4 Ω. Calculate the current.
Continuing: voltmeter across the battery terminals reads what value when I = 1.41 A flows?
In a circuit with R₁ (series) and R₂ ∥ R₃ (parallel), R₃ is suddenly DISCONNECTED. Explain qualitatively what happens to the brightness of R₁.
items.expectedAnswer: Disconnecting R₃ removes a parallel path ⇒ R_parallel INCREASES (only R₂ remains). So R_total INCREASES ⇒ total current DECREASES ⇒ less current flows through R₁ ⇒ R₁ becomes DIMMER.
items.explanation: Removing a parallel branch increases R_parallel and thus R_total. Less current ⇒ less power dissipated in the series resistor ⇒ dimmer.

items.question: If R₁ in the external circuit is INCREASED, what happens to the terminal voltage of the battery? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: If R₁ increases ⇒ R_total increases ⇒ current I decreases. 'Lost voltage' across the internal resistance V_lost = I × r decreases. So V_terminal = ε − Ir INCREASES (gets closer to ε).
items.explanation: Less current ⇒ less voltage dropped internally ⇒ more voltage available externally.

items.question: A battery has external resistors and switches S1 and S2. When S1 is OPEN and S2 is CLOSED, only certain branches conduct, and ammeter A2 reads 3.64 A. The simplified external resistance in this state is 1.42 Ω and the battery has internal resistance r = 0.5 Ω. Calculate the EMF of the battery.

In a circuit with parallel branches controlled by switches, S₂ (controlling one parallel branch) is OPENED. Describe the effect on the (a) ammeter reading in the main line, (b) brightness of a bulb in the remaining parallel branch.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Opening S₂ removes one parallel branch ⇒ external resistance INCREASES ⇒ total current from the battery DECREASES ⇒ main ammeter reading DECREASES. (b) Less current overall means less Ir voltage drop, so terminal voltage INCREASES. The voltage across the remaining parallel branch INCREASES, so MORE current flows through the bulb in it ⇒ bulb gets BRIGHTER.
items.explanation: Removing a parallel branch: R_total ↑, I_total ↓, V_terminal ↑, current in remaining branch ↑, brightness ↑.

items.question: A battery with EMF 9 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω drives a current of 2 A through an external circuit. Calculate the external resistance.
A battery has EMF 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. It is connected to a 2 Ω resistor. Calculate the voltmeter reading across the 2 Ω resistor.
items.explanation: I = 6/(2 + 1) = 2 A. V_R = IR = 2 × 2 = 4 V. (This equals the terminal voltage.)

items.question: A battery is short-circuited (connected directly across its terminals with negligible external resistance). If EMF = 4 V and r = 0.2 Ω, calculate the short-circuit current.
items.explanation: Short circuit: R_ext ≈ 0. I_max = ε/r = 4/0.2 = 20 A. This is the largest current the battery can deliver — usually dangerous (burns out the battery).

items.question: A 12 V battery with r = 0.2 Ω is connected to a circuit. When the main switches are open, only one branch (e.g. with R_Z) carries current and the ammeter reads 1.3 A. Calculate the voltmeter reading across the battery terminals.
A learner says: 'The internal resistance of a battery is fixed at zero in idealised problems.' Is the second part of that statement correct, and what's the point of including a non-zero r?
items.expectedAnswer: An ideal cell has r = 0 (terminal voltage always equals EMF). In practice, real cells have small r > 0, which causes the terminal voltage to DROP when current flows (V_terminal = ε − Ir). Including r in problems reflects real behaviour: dimmer bulbs at high current, heat dissipation in the battery, and limits on maximum current.
items.explanation: Ideal: r = 0. Real: r > 0 causes voltage drop and heating during current flow.
