L7.T1.A3.skill_title: Calculate AC quantities (RMS voltage/current, average power, frequency)
L7.T1.A3.notes: 20 items: 10 lifted, 10 fresh. AC vs DC; V_rms = V_max/√2 and I_rms = I_max/√2; average power P_avg = V_rms × I_rms; period and frequency.

items.question: Consider statements about alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC): I. AC changes direction periodically; II. DC has frequency zero. Which is/are CORRECT?
items.expectedAnswer: Both I and II
items.explanation: Both true: AC reverses direction periodically (50 Hz in SA mains). DC flows in one direction, so it doesn't oscillate — its 'frequency' is zero.

items.question: Define V_rms (root mean square voltage).
items.expectedAnswer: V_rms is the equivalent DC voltage that would produce the same power dissipation in a resistor as the AC voltage does. V_rms = V_max/√2 for a sinusoidal AC waveform.
items.explanation: RMS gives you the 'effective DC equivalent' of an AC. P_avg in a resistor = V_rms²/R = V_rms × I_rms.

items.question: A generator has V_max = 125 V (peak). Calculate V_rms.
Continuing: V_max = 125 V, R = 42.4 Ω. Calculate the maximum (peak) current.
A generator produces V_rms = 200 V and I_max = 6 A. Calculate the resistance of the appliance connected to it.
Continuing: P_avg = V_rms × I_rms. With V_rms = 200 V and I_rms = 4.24 A, calculate the energy dissipated in the appliance in 2 hours.
An AC supply has V_max = 311 V and frequency 50 Hz. Calculate the time t (after t = 0) at which the instantaneous voltage first equals +200 V, given V(t) = V_max sin(2πft).
An AC supply with V_max = 311 V powers a 100 Ω appliance. Calculate the energy dissipated in the appliance in 1 minute.
An AC resistor Y is rated 220 V (rms), 100 W. Calculate the resistance of Y.
items.explanation: P = V_rms²/R ⇒ R = V_rms²/P = 220²/100 = 484 Ω. (Mains AC ratings use RMS values.)

items.question: An AC generator produces a peak voltage of 100 V at frequency f. The speed of rotation is DOUBLED. What happens to the peak voltage and to the period of one rotation?
items.expectedAnswer: Peak V doubles; period halves
items.explanation: Doubling rotation speed doubles f (so T = 1/f halves) and doubles the peak EMF (because peak EMF ∝ ω = 2πf).

items.question: Why are AC mains voltages and currents usually quoted as RMS values rather than peak values?
items.expectedAnswer: RMS values represent the equivalent DC value that would produce the same average power. Multimeters measure RMS, and household appliances (like a 220 V/1500 W kettle) are rated for the AVERAGE power they dissipate, which is calculated using RMS. Peak values are higher (V_peak = √2 × V_rms ≈ 311 V for 220 V mains) and don't directly tell you the power.
items.explanation: Power is what matters in practice; RMS gives consistent power calculations.

items.question: A South African mains supply is 220 V (rms) at 50 Hz. What are the peak voltage and the period of one cycle?
A heater is rated 1500 W at 220 V (rms). Calculate the RMS current and the peak current it draws.
items.explanation: P = V_rms × I_rms ⇒ I_rms = 1500/220 ≈ 6.82 A. I_max = I_rms × √2 ≈ 9.65 A.

items.question: An AC current has I_max = 8 A. What is the RMS current?
A 60 W bulb is connected to a 240 V (rms) AC supply. Calculate the average power dissipated.
items.explanation: The rating is the average power: 60 W. P_avg = V_rms × I_rms = 60 W (by definition of the rated power at the rated voltage).

items.question: Which of the following statements is CORRECT about the peak and RMS values of AC?
options: V_rms and V_peak are equal for sinusoidal AC
items.expectedAnswer: V_peak = V_rms × √2
items.explanation: V_rms = V_max/√2 ⇒ V_peak = V_rms × √2. Equivalently V_peak ≈ 1.414 × V_rms.

items.question: An AC source: V_max = 50 V, R = 25 Ω, f = 60 Hz. Find: (a) V_rms; (b) I_rms; (c) average power dissipated.
items.explanation: V_rms = 50/√2 ≈ 35.36 V. I_rms = V_rms/R ≈ 1.414 A. P = V_rms × I_rms ≈ 50 W (also P = V_max × I_max/2).

items.question: An AC supply has frequency 50 Hz. How long does ONE full cycle take?
A learner asks: 'When AC current alternates direction, doesn't the average current have to be zero?' Briefly explain why P_avg is still nonzero.
items.expectedAnswer: Yes — the AVERAGE current (over a full cycle) is zero, but the average POWER is not. Power = I²R is always positive (current is squared, so both halves of the cycle contribute equally to power). The RMS current squares first, then averages, so I_rms gives the proper effective value for power calculations.
items.explanation: Squaring removes the sign. The 'RMS' construction is exactly designed so I_rms²R = P_avg.

items.question: An AC generator delivers I_max = 2.95 A at frequency 20 Hz. Describe (or sketch) the current vs time graph for TWO complete rotations of the coil.
items.expectedAnswer: Sinusoidal graph with period T = 1/20 = 0.05 s, so two cycles take 0.10 s. Amplitude I_max = 2.95 A. The curve starts at I = 0 at t = 0, rises to +2.95 A at T/4 = 0.0125 s, returns to 0 at T/2 = 0.025 s, falls to −2.95 A at 3T/4 = 0.0375 s, returns to 0 at T = 0.05 s. Repeats once more.
items.explanation: Sinusoidal current; period and amplitude clearly identified; two cycles plotted.

L8.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply Faraday's and Lenz's Laws to calculate induced EMF
L8.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 8 lifted, 12 fresh. Faraday's Law (EMF = -N ΔΦ/Δt); Lenz's Law (induced current opposes the change); EMF calculations with changing flux.

items.question: State FARADAY'S LAW of electromagnetic induction.
items.expectedAnswer: The magnitude of the induced EMF across the ends of a conductor is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage through the conductor: |ε| = N × |ΔΦ/Δt|.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'EMF' + 'rate of change of flux (linkage)'. The N (turns) multiplier matters for coils.

items.question: State LENZ'S LAW.
items.expectedAnswer: The induced current flows in a direction such that the magnetic field it creates OPPOSES the change in magnetic flux that caused it.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'induced current direction' + 'opposes the change in flux'. This is the source of the minus sign in EMF = -N ΔΦ/Δt.

items.question: A bar magnet is thrust QUICKLY into a coil connected to a galvanometer. The galvanometer deflects. Explain why using Faraday's Law.
items.expectedAnswer: As the magnet moves into the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil increases over time. By Faraday's Law, the rate of change of flux induces an EMF in the coil. The EMF drives a current through the galvanometer, causing the deflection.
items.explanation: Change in flux ⇒ induced EMF ⇒ current ⇒ deflection. Direction of deflection is governed by Lenz's Law.

items.question: The magnet is then held STATIONARY inside the coil. What happens to the galvanometer reading and why?
items.expectedAnswer: The galvanometer reads zero. With the magnet stationary, the magnetic flux through the coil is NOT changing (dΦ/dt = 0). By Faraday's Law, ε = 0, so no current flows.
items.explanation: No change in flux ⇒ no induced EMF ⇒ no current. Stationary magnet = no induction.

items.question: State ONE way to INCREASE the induced EMF in a coil where a magnet is being pushed in or out.
items.expectedAnswer: Any one of: (1) Increase the number of turns N in the coil; (2) Move the magnet faster (increase rate of change of flux, Δt smaller); (3) Use a stronger magnet (higher B); (4) Increase the area of the coil.
items.explanation: ε = -N × ΔΦ/Δt. Increasing N, B, A, or speed (smaller Δt) all increase induced EMF.

items.question: A rectangular coil of N = 400 turns, area A = 0.05 m², rotates in a uniform magnetic field B = 0.8 T at 50 revolutions per second. Calculate the peak (maximum) induced EMF.
An AC generator produces an alternating EMF described by ε(t) = 200 sin(100πt) volts. Write down the peak EMF and the frequency.
items.explanation: ε = ε_max sin(ωt). ε_max = 200 V (amplitude). ω = 100π = 2πf ⇒ f = 50 Hz.

items.question: A 200-turn coil of area 0.04 m² is placed in a magnetic field. The field changes from 0.5 T to 1.5 T in 0.2 s. Calculate the magnitude of the induced EMF (assume field is perpendicular to the coil).
A 50-turn coil has the flux through each turn changed from 2 × 10⁻³ Wb to 8 × 10⁻³ Wb in 0.05 s. Calculate the induced EMF.
Define MAGNETIC FLUX through a coil.
items.expectedAnswer: Magnetic flux Φ = B × A × cosθ, where B is the magnetic field strength, A is the coil area, and θ is the angle between B and the area's normal. SI unit: weber (Wb = T·m²). Flux measures the 'amount' of magnetic field passing through the area.
items.explanation: Φ depends on B, A and angle. When B is perpendicular to coil (θ = 0), Φ = BA (maximum).

items.question: A bar magnet is pushed INTO a coil. The induced current creates a magnetic pole at the near end of the coil that REPELS the incoming magnet. This is an example of:
items.expectedAnswer: Lenz's Law
items.explanation: Lenz's Law: the induced current opposes the change. Pushing in a magnet ⇒ flux increases ⇒ induced current creates a field that REPELS the magnet (tries to keep flux unchanged).

items.question: If you PULL a magnet OUT of a coil, what type of magnetic pole forms at the near end of the coil (due to the induced current)?
items.expectedAnswer: An opposite pole. As the magnet is withdrawn, flux DECREASES; by Lenz's Law, the induced current produces a magnetic field that OPPOSES the change — meaning it tries to maintain the original flux. So the near end of the coil acts like the OPPOSITE pole of the magnet (attracting it, resisting the withdrawal).
items.explanation: Lenz applied to withdrawal: induced current tries to KEEP the magnet (attract it back). If you pull out an N pole, the near end of the coil acts like a S pole.

items.question: Which of the following will INDUCE an EMF in a closed coil?
options: A constant magnetic field through the coil
A magnet held stationary inside the coil
A magnet moving relative to the coil
A coil at rest in zero magnetic field
items.expectedAnswer: A magnet moving relative to the coil
items.explanation: Induction requires a CHANGE in flux. Only relative motion of magnet and coil (or a changing field) creates that change.

items.question: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.01 m² is initially perpendicular to a 0.6 T magnetic field. The coil is rotated 90° in 0.05 s so that its plane is parallel to the field (no flux). Calculate the average induced EMF.
A learner says: 'Faraday's Law shows that a larger magnetic field always produces a larger induced EMF.' Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Not by itself. EMF depends on the RATE OF CHANGE of flux (ΔΦ/Δt), not just the field strength. A huge but unchanging magnetic field induces ZERO EMF. To increase EMF you must change the field, area, orientation, or number of turns — and how QUICKLY this change occurs matters.
items.explanation: Critical distinction: induction requires change. Big B with no change ⇒ no induced EMF.

items.question: What does the MINUS SIGN in EMF = −N × ΔΦ/Δt represent?
items.expectedAnswer: It encodes LENZ'S LAW: the induced EMF (and current) acts in a direction such that it OPPOSES the change in flux that caused it. The minus sign ensures the induced current creates a magnetic field opposing the flux change.
items.explanation: Lenz's Law via the minus sign. Direction of induced current is set by this sign convention.

items.question: A coil of 500 turns has flux per turn change from 0 to 4 × 10⁻⁴ Wb in 0.01 s. Find the induced EMF.
How does INCREASING THE NUMBER OF TURNS in a coil affect the induced EMF (with all other factors equal)?
items.expectedAnswer: Increases EMF proportionally
items.explanation: ε ∝ N (each turn contributes its own induced EMF; they add). Doubling N doubles ε.

items.question: A coil of 200 turns and area 0.025 m² is rotated in a 0.4 T magnetic field at 30 revolutions per second. Calculate the peak induced EMF.
An induction stove transfers energy to a metal pot. Briefly explain (using Faraday's/Lenz's Law) why an induction stove cannot heat a wooden spoon.
items.expectedAnswer: Induction heating uses a rapidly changing magnetic field to induce eddy currents in conductors. Metal pots (conductors) experience induced currents which dissipate heat through their resistance. A wooden spoon is an INSULATOR — no free charges to form currents, so no induced currents, no heat. (Same reason: Faraday's Law produces an EMF in any conductor, but only conductors can carry the resulting current.)
items.explanation: Eddy current heating requires free charges (conductor). Insulators have no induced currents to dissipate energy.

L8.T1.A2.skill_title: Describe AC and DC generators and motors
L8.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 12 lifted, 8 fresh. AC vs DC generators (slip rings vs split-ring commutator); motors (electrical → mechanical); generator energy conversion; uses of right-hand and Fleming's rules.

items.question: What is the function of the SPLIT-RING COMMUTATOR in a DC electric motor?
options: Maintains contact with the slip rings to produce AC output
Steps down the voltage by half each cycle
Reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half rotation
Stores charge from the battery between rotations
items.expectedAnswer: Reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half rotation
items.explanation: Split-ring commutator: at the moment the coil crosses the field's normal, it flips the contact, reversing the coil current — so the torque stays in the SAME rotational direction (continuous rotation in one direction).

items.question: An electrical machine has SLIP RINGS (not a commutator). What type of machine is this?
items.expectedAnswer: AC generator
items.explanation: Slip rings = continuous contact ⇒ output current alternates (AC). DC machines use split-ring commutators to convert to one direction.

items.question: State the ENERGY CONVERSION that takes place in a DC MOTOR.
items.expectedAnswer: Electrical energy is converted into mechanical (kinetic) energy.
items.explanation: Motors: electrical IN → mechanical OUT. Generators: mechanical IN → electrical OUT.

items.question: State the ENERGY CONVERSION in an AC generator.
items.expectedAnswer: Mechanical (kinetic) energy is converted into electrical energy.
items.explanation: Generator: mechanical → electrical. Mechanical input (rotating coil) ⇒ induced EMF (electrical output).

items.question: Does a DC motor use AC or DC current at its input?
items.expectedAnswer: DC (direct current).
items.explanation: DC motor takes DC input; the commutator handles the internal current reversal to keep torque continuous.

items.question: State the function of the COMMUTATOR in a DC motor.
items.expectedAnswer: The commutator reverses the direction of current in the coil every half rotation, ensuring the coil continues to rotate in one direction.
items.explanation: Same role as in DC generator: split-ring contact flip provides continuous one-direction torque.

items.question: To CHANGE the direction of rotation of a DC motor, which TWO of the following can be done? (i) Swap the north and south poles of the magnets; (ii) Increase the supply voltage; (iii) Reverse the current direction (swap battery terminals).
items.expectedAnswer: (i) and (iii)
items.explanation: Reversing magnetic poles or reversing the current both reverse the torque direction (force on each wire reverses). Increasing voltage only makes it spin faster, not in the opposite direction.

items.question: Give TWO ways in which the MAXIMUM EMF of an AC generator can be INCREASED.
items.expectedAnswer: Any TWO of: (1) Increase the SPEED of rotation; (2) Increase the NUMBER OF TURNS in the coil; (3) Use a STRONGER magnetic field (larger B); (4) Increase the AREA of the coil; (5) Use a soft-iron core to concentrate the flux.
items.explanation: ε_max = NBAω. Any factor that increases N, B, A, or ω increases the peak EMF.

items.question: In an AC generator diagram, a rotating coil contacts the external circuit through component X. Name component X.
items.expectedAnswer: Slip rings.
items.explanation: Slip rings = pair of complete rings that maintain continuous electrical contact with the brushes; allow AC output.

items.question: State the function of the BRUSHES in a generator.
items.expectedAnswer: The brushes maintain electrical contact between the rotating slip rings (or commutator) and the stationary external circuit, allowing current to flow from the coil to the external circuit.
items.explanation: Brushes are stationary; slip rings/commutator rotate against them. They bridge the rotating coil to the fixed external wires.

items.question: Explain how an EMF is induced in the rotating coil of an AC generator (using Faraday's Law).
items.expectedAnswer: As the coil rotates between the magnetic poles, the magnetic flux through the coil changes continuously with time (Φ = BA cos(ωt)). By Faraday's Law, a changing flux induces an EMF in the coil: ε = -N dΦ/dt = NBA ω sin(ωt). The EMF varies sinusoidally with the coil's angular position.
items.explanation: Generator output is sinusoidal because flux varies cosinusoidally with time (as the coil rotates) and Faraday's Law gives ε = -dΦ/dt.

items.question: State ONE difference between an AC generator and a DC generator.
items.expectedAnswer: Any one of: AC generator uses SLIP RINGS and produces an alternating (sinusoidal) current/voltage. DC generator uses a SPLIT-RING COMMUTATOR, which reverses the polarity of the output every half cycle so that the output is always in the same direction (pulsating DC).
items.explanation: Key difference: slip rings (AC) vs split-ring commutator (DC). Output: alternating vs same-direction.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of a typical AC generator?
items.expectedAnswer: Split-ring commutator
items.explanation: AC generators use slip rings (continuous contact for both directions). Split-ring commutators belong to DC generators / motors.

items.question: A DC motor and a DC generator are essentially the SAME machine. Which differs between them?
items.expectedAnswer: Direction of energy conversion (electrical ↔ mechanical)
items.explanation: Same hardware (coil, magnets, brushes, commutator). Motor: electrical → mechanical. Generator: mechanical → electrical. They're each other's inverse.

items.question: On the EMF-vs-time output of an AC generator, what does the PEAK value correspond to physically?
items.expectedAnswer: The peak EMF occurs when the coil's plane is PARALLEL to the magnetic field (and the area normal is perpendicular to B). At that instant the rate of change of flux is largest, so ε is maximum. ε_peak = NBAω.
items.explanation: Peak EMF when coil is moving through the field at maximum perpendicular speed. Flux is changing fastest at that orientation.

items.question: How does the OUTPUT of a DC generator (with a split-ring commutator) differ from that of an AC generator on a V-t graph?
items.expectedAnswer: AC generator: sinusoidal output that alternates between positive and negative values. DC generator: pulsating DC — the negative half-cycle is flipped to positive by the commutator, so the output is always positive (looks like the absolute value of a sine wave).
items.explanation: DC commutator flips every half-cycle ⇒ rectifies AC waveform to one polarity. Output is pulsating DC, not pure DC.

items.question: A DC motor 'runs as a generator' (back-EMF) when its coil rotates. How does this back-EMF affect the current drawn by the motor?
items.expectedAnswer: When the motor's coil rotates, it produces an induced EMF (back-EMF) that OPPOSES the supply voltage (Lenz's Law). The net voltage driving current is the supply minus the back-EMF, so the current DECREASES as the motor speeds up. This explains why motors draw a large current at startup (no back-EMF) and less when running at full speed.
items.explanation: Back-EMF is a Lenz-Law phenomenon: induction opposes the change. Net V = V_supply − ε_back ⇒ less I at higher speed.

items.question: Which of the following statements about generators and motors is CORRECT?
options: Generators convert mechanical to chemical energy
Motors convert electrical to mechanical energy
Generators convert mechanical to mechanical energy
Motors convert electrical to electrical energy
items.expectedAnswer: Motors convert electrical to mechanical energy
items.explanation: Motors: electrical → mechanical. Generators: mechanical → electrical.

items.question: Sketch (in words) an EMF-vs-time graph for TWO complete rotations of an AC generator coil. What characterises this output?
items.expectedAnswer: Sinusoidal wave. Two complete cycles shown (i.e. two peaks above and two troughs below the time axis). Peak EMF ε_max labelled on the y-axis. Period T = 1/f marked on the time axis. The waveform alternates between +ε_max and −ε_max, repeating every T.
items.explanation: Sinusoidal AC output. Peaks every half cycle, alternating sign.

items.question: Why does an electric motor experience a TORQUE on its current-carrying coil in a magnetic field?
items.expectedAnswer: Each side of the coil carries current in opposite directions. The magnetic field exerts a force F = BIL on each side (Fleming's left-hand / motor rule). These two forces act in opposite directions on opposite sides of the coil, creating a turning effect (torque) about the coil's rotation axis. The torque causes the coil to spin.
items.explanation: Two opposite forces on opposite sides of the coil ⇒ couple ⇒ torque. This is what spins the motor.

L9.T1.A1.skill_title: Apply the photoelectric effect (work function, threshold frequency, max KE)
L9.T1.A1.notes: 20 items: 13 lifted, 7 fresh. Photoelectric effect definition + calculations: E = hf, W₀ = hf₀, E_k(max) = hf − W₀; threshold frequency; effects of intensity vs frequency.

items.question: Define the PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT.
items.expectedAnswer: The photoelectric effect is the process whereby electrons are ejected from the surface of a metal when electromagnetic radiation of sufficient frequency (above the threshold) shines on it.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'electrons ejected from metal surface' + 'EM radiation of sufficient frequency'.

items.question: Define the WORK FUNCTION of a metal.
items.expectedAnswer: The work function (W₀) is the MINIMUM energy needed to eject an electron from the surface of a metal.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'minimum energy' + 'eject electron from surface'. W₀ = h × f₀ (threshold frequency).

items.question: A photon has energy E. If the frequency of the photon is doubled, its energy becomes:
items.expectedAnswer: 2E
items.explanation: E = hf — energy is directly proportional to frequency. Doubling f doubles E.

items.question: A photon has energy 2X joules. The work function of the metal is X joules. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectron?
items.expectedAnswer: X
items.explanation: E_k(max) = E_photon − W₀ = 2X − X = X J.

items.question: The threshold frequency of a metal is f₀. If light of frequency 2f₀ shines on the surface, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons is:
items.expectedAnswer: hf₀
items.explanation: E_k = hf − W₀ = h(2f₀) − hf₀ = hf₀.

items.question: The photoelectric effect is best explained by treating light as:
items.expectedAnswer: A particle (photon)
items.explanation: Einstein's photon model: light is quantised into discrete packets (photons) of energy hf. The wave model alone cannot explain the threshold-frequency dependence.

items.question: Which phenomenon provides evidence that LIGHT has a PARTICLE nature?
items.expectedAnswer: Photoelectric effect
items.explanation: Photoelectric effect shows light comes in quanta (photons). Diffraction, interference and refraction all support the wave nature.

items.question: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz shines on a zinc surface (W₀ = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). Calculate the energy of ONE photon of the incident light. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.)
Continuing: photon energy = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, W₀ (zinc) = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons OR explain if none are emitted.
items.expectedAnswer: E_k = E_photon − W₀ = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ = −1.58 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. A negative result means the photon energy is LESS than the work function. So NO photoelectrons are emitted. The light frequency is below the threshold frequency of zinc.
items.explanation: If hf < W₀, no electrons are emitted at all. Negative 'KE' is unphysical — the answer is 'no emission'.

items.question: Calculate the threshold frequency of zinc (W₀ = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s).
The intensity of light incident on a metal surface (above threshold) is DOUBLED. What is the effect on the MAXIMUM KINETIC ENERGY of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.expectedAnswer: E_k(max) REMAINS THE SAME. Intensity determines the NUMBER of photons per second (and hence the number of electrons emitted per second), but each electron absorbs only ONE photon. The maximum KE depends only on the frequency of the light (E_k = hf − W₀), not on intensity.
items.explanation: Critical concept. Intensity controls electron NUMBER; frequency controls electron ENERGY.

items.question: Caesium is illuminated with light of wavelength λ = 4.7 × 10⁻⁷ m. The threshold frequency of caesium f₀ = 4.37 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the maximum speed of the ejected photoelectrons. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴, c = 3 × 10⁸, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.)
Light of frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz is incident on a metal with W₀ = 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the maximum SPEED of the photoelectrons. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴, m_e = 9.11×10⁻³¹.)
The threshold frequency for metal A is 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the work function of metal A. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.)

In a photoelectric experiment with light above threshold frequency: if the INTENSITY of the light is INCREASED (at the same frequency), what happens to the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons?
items.expectedAnswer: Remains the same
items.explanation: Intensity does NOT affect E_k(max). Only frequency does.

items.question: Continuing: if the INTENSITY is increased at the same frequency, what happens to the NUMBER OF PHOTOELECTRONS ejected per second?
items.expectedAnswer: Increases
items.explanation: Higher intensity ⇒ more photons per second ⇒ more electrons ejected per second.

items.question: Light of frequency 1.2 × 10¹⁵ Hz shines on a metal. The total energy absorbed by the metal per second is 1.75 × 10⁻⁹ J. Calculate the NUMBER of photons per second incident on the metal. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴.)
UV light shines on a negatively-charged zinc plate in an electroscope. Explain why the gold leaf COLLAPSES.
items.expectedAnswer: UV photons have frequency above the threshold frequency of zinc, so they have enough energy to eject electrons from the zinc plate (photoelectric effect). The negatively-charged plate progressively loses electrons, reducing its negative charge. As the plate becomes less negative, the gold leaf is less repelled and FALLS BACK toward the stem (collapses).
items.explanation: UV ⇒ photoelectrons ejected ⇒ plate loses negative charge ⇒ less repulsion ⇒ leaf falls.

items.question: If GREEN light (at higher intensity than the original UV) replaces the UV on the same zinc electroscope, will the leaf collapse? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: NO. Green light has a LOWER frequency than UV, BELOW the threshold frequency of zinc. No photoelectric emission occurs, no matter how intense the green light is. Higher intensity provides more photons but each photon still has insufficient energy individually (hf < W₀). The leaf will not collapse.
items.explanation: Frequency is what matters for ejection. Below threshold ⇒ no emission, regardless of intensity.

items.question: On a graph of E_k(max) (y-axis) versus frequency f (x-axis) for a photoelectric experiment with a given metal, what do (a) the gradient, (b) the x-intercept, and (c) the y-intercept represent?
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Gradient = Planck's constant h ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. (b) x-intercept = threshold frequency f₀ (where E_k = 0). (c) y-intercept = −W₀ (the negative of the work function; the line is E_k = hf − W₀, so when f = 0, E_k = −W₀ — but this part of the graph is unphysical because no emission occurs below f₀).
items.explanation: E_k = hf − W₀ ⇒ linear graph with gradient h and x-intercept f₀.

L9.T1.A2.notes: 20 items: 5 lifted, 15 fresh. Atomic energy levels; emission spectra (electrons drop to lower level, photon emitted); absorption spectra (electrons absorb photons, dark lines); identification of elements; line spectra are discrete.

items.question: Explain how an EMISSION SPECTRUM is formed.
items.expectedAnswer: When electrons in excited atoms drop from higher to lower energy levels, they emit photons with specific energies E = hf = E_high − E_low. Each transition produces a photon of a particular frequency (or wavelength). The collection of all possible transitions in an atom produces a series of bright (emission) lines at characteristic wavelengths — the emission spectrum.
items.explanation: Bright-line spectrum: high → low transition emits photon of energy = ΔE. Discrete because energy levels are discrete.

items.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes an ABSORPTION spectrum?
options: Bright lines on a black background
Dark lines on a continuous (rainbow) background
A single line at the threshold frequency
A continuous rainbow with no lines
items.expectedAnswer: Dark lines on a continuous (rainbow) background
items.explanation: Absorption: continuous light passing through cold gas, photons matching ΔE between levels are absorbed, leaving dark lines at those wavelengths.

items.question: An atom has four energy levels E₁, E₂, E₃ and E₄ (with E₁ lowest). Which downward transition will produce the photon with the LOWEST frequency?
items.expectedAnswer: E₄ to E₃
items.explanation: Lowest frequency = smallest photon energy = smallest energy gap between levels. The transition between two ADJACENT high levels (E₄ to E₃) usually has the smallest ΔE.

items.question: An electron in an atom moves from energy level x to energy level y (where y > x, i.e. higher energy). Which statement is CORRECT?
options: A photon is emitted with energy y − x
A photon is absorbed with energy y − x
A photon is emitted with energy y + x
items.expectedAnswer: A photon is absorbed with energy y − x
items.explanation: Moving UP in energy levels requires absorbing a photon of exactly the energy difference ΔE = y − x. Moving DOWN emits a photon.

items.question: An electron in a hydrogen atom drops from the n = 3 level (E₃ = −2.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) to the n = 2 level (E₂ = −5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). Calculate the frequency of the emitted photon. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴.)
Why are atomic emission and absorption spectra DISCRETE (line spectra) rather than continuous?
items.expectedAnswer: Atoms have DISCRETE energy levels — electrons can only occupy specific energies. A transition between two levels has a specific ΔE, so the photon emitted (or absorbed) has a specific frequency f = ΔE/h. Only certain frequencies appear ⇒ discrete lines. A continuous spectrum would require electrons to have any energy, which they don't in isolated atoms.
items.explanation: Quantisation of energy levels ⇒ quantisation of photon frequencies.

items.question: An emission spectrum has THREE bright lines. What does this tell you about the number of possible electron transitions in the atom?
items.expectedAnswer: Three downward transitions are responsible for the three lines. If the atom has n energy levels, the maximum number of distinct emission lines is n(n−1)/2 (all pairs). Three lines could come from, e.g., three transitions among 3 levels (3·2/2 = 3 transitions: 3→1, 3→2, 2→1).
items.explanation: Three lines ⇔ three transitions. For 3 levels there are exactly 3 possible transitions.

items.question: How can astronomers identify the composition of a distant star using its absorption spectrum?
items.expectedAnswer: Each element has a unique 'fingerprint' of absorption lines at known wavelengths. By matching the dark lines in a star's continuous spectrum to laboratory-measured absorption lines of various elements, astronomers can identify which elements are present in the star's atmosphere.
items.explanation: Spectroscopic fingerprinting: each element has unique discrete wavelengths. Astronomy uses this for compositional analysis.

items.question: Which of the following is TRUE about emission and absorption spectra of the SAME element?
options: They have completely different sets of wavelengths
Emission and absorption lines occur at the SAME wavelengths (one bright, one dark)
Emission has more lines than absorption
Absorption only shows visible light; emission shows all
items.expectedAnswer: Emission and absorption lines occur at the SAME wavelengths (one bright, one dark)
items.explanation: Same transitions ⇒ same wavelengths. Emission: photon RELEASED at λ; absorption: photon REMOVED at λ. The dark lines in absorption match the bright lines in emission, for the same element.

items.question: In a HYDROGEN emission spectrum, you observe bright lines in the visible region. These are part of the:
items.expectedAnswer: Balmer series (visible)
items.explanation: Balmer series = transitions ending at n = 2, with lines in the visible spectrum. Lyman ends at n = 1 (UV). Paschen at n = 3 (IR).

items.question: A learner says: 'Atoms emit ALL frequencies of light continuously.' Is this correct? Briefly explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. Atoms emit only DISCRETE wavelengths corresponding to the differences between their quantised energy levels. A heated solid (like an incandescent bulb filament) can emit a continuous spectrum due to many overlapping interactions, but ISOLATED atoms in a gas produce only line spectra at specific wavelengths.
items.explanation: Continuous vs line spectrum: solids ⇒ continuous; gases (isolated atoms) ⇒ line.

items.question: An atom has energy levels at E₁ = 0, E₂ = 3.0 eV, E₃ = 6.5 eV. How many DIFFERENT photon energies could it emit?
items.explanation: Possible transitions: 3→1 (6.5 eV), 3→2 (3.5 eV), 2→1 (3.0 eV) = 3 distinct photon energies.

items.question: Continuing: of the three transitions in the previous question, which produces the LONGEST wavelength photon?
items.expectedAnswer: The 2 → 1 transition (smallest ΔE = 3.0 eV). Longest wavelength ⇔ smallest photon energy (E = hc/λ; smaller E ⇒ larger λ).
items.explanation: Inverse relationship: small ΔE → long λ. The 2→1 transition has the smallest energy gap.

items.question: What does each DARK LINE in the absorption spectrum of a star tell you?
items.expectedAnswer: Each dark line corresponds to a specific wavelength where photons (from the continuous solar/starlight) have been absorbed by atoms in the star's (cooler) outer atmosphere. The wavelength of each dark line matches a transition between two energy levels in a particular element, so the pattern of dark lines identifies which elements are present.
items.explanation: Dark lines = absorbed wavelengths. Each one identifies an element through its known transition wavelengths.

items.question: An electron in an atom absorbs a photon and jumps from n = 1 to n = 3. The energy levels are E₁ = −13.6 eV and E₃ = −1.51 eV. Calculate the wavelength of the absorbed photon. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴, c = 3×10⁸, 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J.)
Why is sodium street lighting YELLOW?
items.expectedAnswer: Sodium vapour emits strongly in the yellow region of the visible spectrum (a 'doublet' near 589 nm) when its electrons drop between specific energy levels. The dominant transitions correspond to yellow light, so a sodium lamp appears yellow.
items.explanation: Sodium D-lines: 589 nm doublet. Bright, narrow yellow emission characteristic of sodium.

items.question: A continuous spectrum is observed from an incandescent bulb. When the light passes through cold hydrogen gas, dark lines appear at the SAME wavelengths as the hydrogen Balmer emission lines. Why?
items.expectedAnswer: The cold hydrogen gas absorbs photons of exactly the energies corresponding to transitions FROM the n = 2 level UP to higher levels (the Balmer transitions in reverse). These specific wavelengths are removed from the transmitted light, producing dark lines exactly where hydrogen would normally EMIT in its emission spectrum.
items.explanation: Same transitions absorb (cold) and emit (hot) at the same wavelengths — Kirchhoff's reciprocity.

items.question: Which of the following BEST describes an EMISSION spectrum?
options: Dark lines on a continuous rainbow
Bright coloured lines on a dark background
A continuous rainbow with no lines
Only one bright line, regardless of element
items.expectedAnswer: Bright coloured lines on a dark background
items.explanation: Emission: discrete bright lines (each from an electron transition) on an otherwise dark background.

items.question: A hydrogen emission spectrum has several distinct lines. What CHANGES between hydrogen at room temperature and hydrogen at very high temperature?
items.expectedAnswer: At higher temperatures, more atoms are excited to higher energy levels (more thermal energy ⇒ more populated upper states). So the higher-frequency emission lines (corresponding to transitions from higher upper states) become BRIGHTER (more electrons available to make those transitions). The set of wavelengths remains the same — only the intensities change.
items.explanation: Temperature affects intensity (population), not the line positions (set by atomic structure).

items.question: Explain the difference between an EMISSION spectrum and an ABSORPTION spectrum in one or two sentences each.
items.expectedAnswer: Emission: bright lines on a dark background, produced when electrons in excited atoms drop from high to low energy levels and emit photons. Absorption: dark lines on a continuous rainbow background, produced when atoms absorb specific photons matching their energy-level differences. Same atom ⇒ same wavelengths but inverted in appearance.
items.explanation: Bright vs dark; same wavelengths for the same element; emission = drop, absorption = jump.
